7 · THE ANSWER IN DEGREE TWO

Mostly squares, with a small remainder

The inequalities on gm act like exchange rates. The question left is which mix of cycles, with total length n, makes the product of normalized factors smallest, since that graph is slowest at every time and hence in expectation.

For n ≥ 3, define

8 · EVERY DEGREE

Kd,d beats cliques by a log log term

Degree two might look special, so the paper also shows the conjecture fails for every fixed d ≥ 2, by comparing unions of Kd,d with unions of Kd+1 directly.

The square argument generalizes. In Bn,d = (n/(2d))Kd,d there are m = n/d classes of d vertices, a sample from a class covers a vertex of the opposite class until it is full, and so the graph is covered exactly when every class has been sampled d times:

Fact · Proposition 5.1

For n divisible by both 2d and d + 1, as n → ∞,

So the Kd,d union is slower than the clique union for all large enough such n.

Eq. 26

The log log term is the price of needing d copies of each class in Section 1. A clique's last vertex waits at rate d once, but a Kd,d class of twins makes the process wait at rate d up to d times. Proposition 5.1 is asymptotic and does not say where the crossover happens for d ≥ 3. As our own check at the first common order for d = 3, n = 12, the exact chain gives cc(2K3,3) ≈ 19.566 against cc(3K4) ≈ 18.670, so K3,3 already wins there.

The paper also refutes Alon's uniform estimate, Eq. 31. Proposition 5.2 shows that for every m ≥ 2,

so cc(2Km) ≥ 2m + √m. Two cliques of size m form an (m − 1)-regular graph on n = 2m vertices, and their excess over n grows like √m while (n log n)/d stays of order log m, so no absolute constant works. The source of the √m is imbalance: after 2m samples, one clique has typically received about √m fewer than it needs. With m = 3 the bracket is 6 + 6 · 20/64 = 7.875, and our exact value cc(2K3) = 9.22 sits 1.345 above it, inside the allowed 3/2.

In short: for every fixed d ≥ 2, unions of Kd,d beat unions of Kd+1 by about ((d − 1)/d) n log log n, and two cliques already break the suggested uniform bound.

10 · ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what isn't

The degree-two results are complete and, by the standards of the field, elementary: Poissonization, an exact rate identity, a backward duality on cycles, and power-series coefficient comparisons. The twelve-vertex counterexample is a finite computation and is easy to trust; our independent rational-arithmetic solution of the 4,096-state chain reproduces both of the paper's fractions exactly, and also confirms C6 and 2C3 tie and that C4 ⊔ C5 beats 3K3. The full classification rests on Lemmas 3.1 to 3.3, which are compact but careful; we checked the generating-function formula only for m = 2 and 3, and the inequalities numerically at four times, not in general.

Several claims are narrower than the headline. In degree d ≥ 3 the paper does not find the slowest graph at each order. Theorem 4.4 identifies Kd,d unions as optimal only among graphs whose components have bounded size L and only for n beyond an unspecified threshold depending on d and L, so a graph with one huge component is not covered. Proposition 5.1 disproves the conjecture only for large n, with an unspecified Od(n) error, and does not say where the crossover is. Graphs that are not regular are outside the scope except for Theorem 4.1, which applies to any graph with minimum degree at least one.

The paper states that the authors used a large language model during preparation, for mathematical exploration, checking arguments, organization and language editing, and that the authors take responsibility for the statements and proofs. It is a fresh preprint and has not been refereed.

A connection, oursThe mechanism in Section 5 is general: when a process ends with several items that can only be served by the same bottleneck, the waiting times stack and the tail picks up a polynomial factor. The same thing makes a sum of k exponential service times (an Erlang distribution) far more likely to run long than a single exponential with the same rate. The paper doesn't make this connection.

In short: degree two is settled completely and verifiably; higher degree is settled only asymptotically and within bounded component sizes.

FURTHER READING

Deng and Wang, Extremal Graphs for Alon's Graph Coupon-Collector Conjecture (2026). The paper.

Doumas and Papanicolaou, The Coupon Collector's Problem Revisited: Generalizing the Double Dixie Cup Problem of Newman and Shepp (2015). Its introduction is a readable survey of the coupon collector and the repeated version behind Eq. 9, including the Erdős–Rényi limit law.

The paper's other background sources, Alon's "Problems and results in extremal combinatorics II" (Discrete Mathematics, 2008), Newman and Shepp's "The double Dixie cup problem" (1960) and Durrett's Essentials of Stochastic Processes, could not be opened from here and are listed without links.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.11345v1. Equation, lemma and theorem numbers match the paper. Both animations run real computations: the covering process step by step on the triangle and square, and the exact distribution functions q(t)6 and r(t)4 with numerically integrated tails. The step-by-step derivation of cc(K3), the integral for cc(C4), the checks of Eq. 19, the g-table, the exact small-n values and the 2K3,3 versus 3K4 comparison are ours.

Exact (Non-)Accelerations of Heavy-Ball Discretizations

Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Takáč · posted Nov 10, 2026 · math.OC · arXiv 2611.13584

Overview

Two momentum methods can follow the same differential equation in the limit and still behave completely differently: one converges fast on every smooth convex bowl, the other can circle forever on some of them, and the deciding quantity is whether the gradient is evaluated at least half a step ahead of the current point. This paper makes that precise for the whole family of two-step momentum methods that includes Polyak's heavy ball, Nesterov's accelerated method and the triple momentum method. It computes the exact worst-case speed of each method when the problem is badly conditioned, finds that the answer is the smaller of two numbers, θ/3 and a quadratic constant, explains where the 1/3 comes from, and shows that any method that looks less than half a step ahead cannot be accelerated on general functions.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • why gradient descent crawls in a narrow valley, and how the condition number κ = L/μ sets its speed at (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) per step;
  • the momentum family, its characteristic polynomial, and why Polyak's tuning reaches the rate 1/2 on a valley with κ = 9;
  • how a momentum method with β close to 1 turns into a damped oscillator, ẍ + θẋ + ∇F(x) = 0, and why its speed on quadratics is the constant cQ;
  • the energy argument that limits the oscillator to the rate θ/3 on non-quadratic functions, and the spiraling trajectories that show θ/3 cannot be beaten;
  • the half-step identity behind the wall τ = 1/2, and why heavy ball (τ = 0) can fall into a 3-cycle on a perfectly nice function;
  • the exact constants of Nesterov's method (2/3), its best tuning (√(2/3)) and the triple momentum method (1), and what the paper proves versus what remains open.
notationSymbols used throughout
f, x⋆
the function to minimize and its unique minimizer; we shift so that x⋆ = 0
μ, L
strong convexity and smoothness: every curvature of f lies between μ and L
κ, ε
the condition number κ = L/μ, and ε = κ−1/2, the small parameter of the paper
𝓕μ,L
the class of all μ-strongly convex functions with L-Lipschitz gradient
h, β, τ
step size, momentum, and extrapolation (how far ahead the gradient is evaluated)
x̃k
the query point, where the gradient is evaluated at step k
χλ(z)
the characteristic polynomial of the method on a quadratic with curvature λ
ρq, ρ𝓕
the worst rate per step over quadratics, and over the whole class 𝓕μ,L
θ, y
the slow data: β = 1 − θ/√κ and hL → y
cQ, c𝓕
the leading constants in 1 − c/√κ on quadratics and on the whole class
ω, ξ
a frequency in [0, π] and ξ = 1 − cos ω
Θ(ω)
the spectral phase of the method at frequency ω; Θ(ω)/ω is its phase lead in steps
Two running examples
  • The κ = 9 valley. The quadratic f(x) = ½(x12 + 9x22) in the plane, so μ = 1, L = 9 and √κ = 3. Every method in the paper has round numbers here: gradient descent contracts by 0.8 per step, Polyak's heavy ball by 1/2, and the triple momentum method by 2/3.
  • The two oscillators. The damped equation ẍ + θẋ + mx = 0 with (θ, m) = (2, 1) and with (θ, m) = (3, 2). The first is the slow limit of Nesterov's method, the second that of the triple momentum method. Their decay rates, 1 and 1 on quadratics but 2/3 and 1 on general functions, are the paper's headline numbers in miniature.
1 · GRADIENT DESCENT AND THE CONDITION NUMBER

Why is a narrow valley slow?

Everything in the paper is measured against plain gradient descent, so it is worth seeing exactly why gradient descent is slow and what number controls it. The answer is the ratio between the steepest and the flattest curvature of the function.

Definition · the class 𝓕μ,L and the condition number

A differentiable function f belongs to 𝓕μ,L, with 0 < μ < L, when f(x) − (μ/2)‖x‖2 is convex and the gradient is L-Lipschitz, ‖∇f(x) − ∇f(x′)‖ ≤ L‖x − x′‖. The condition number is κ = L/μ.

In words: f is a bowl that curves upward at least as fast as μ and at most as fast as L in every direction, and κ measures how elongated the bowl can be.

For a quadratic the curvatures are literally the eigenvalues. Take f(x) = ½ Σi λixi2 with μ ≤ λi ≤ L. The gradient has coordinates λixi, so one step of gradient descent with step h acts on each coordinate separately,

standard; background, not in the paper

The flat direction wants a large step and the steep direction a small one. Balancing the two worst factors, |1 − hμ| = |1 − hL|, gives h = 2/(μ + L) and the contraction

derivationWhy is 2/(μ + L) the best fixed step?

The function λ ↦ |1 − hλ| is a V-shape with its zero at λ = 1/h, so its maximum over [μ, L] is attained at an endpoint and equals max(|1 − hμ|, |1 − hL|). Increasing h lowers the first and raises the second once hL > 1, so the maximum is smallest where they are equal. That happens when 1 − hμ = hL − 1, that is h = 2/(μ + L), and the common value is 1 − 2μ/(μ + L) = (L − μ)/(L + μ). Dividing top and bottom by μ gives (κ − 1)/(κ + 1).

∎

On the κ = 9 valley, h = 2/10 = 0.2, and the two coordinates are multiplied by 1 − 0.2 = 0.8 and 1 − 1.8 = −0.8 at every step. The steep coordinate flips sign each step while the flat one creeps toward zero, and the distance to the minimum shrinks by exactly 0.8 per step. Reaching one millionth of the starting distance takes about ln(106)/ln(1/0.8) ≈ 62 steps.

Fact

Gradient descent needs on the order of κ steps to gain each constant factor of accuracy. The whole subject of acceleration is the search for methods that need only on the order of √κ, which is a large saving when κ is in the thousands or millions.

In short: curvature spread κ forces gradient descent to rate (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) ≈ 1 − 2/κ, which is 0.8 on the running valley.

2 · THE MOMENTUM FAMILY

What does adding momentum buy?

A ball rolling down the valley does not stop and restart at every step; it remembers its velocity, which smooths out the zigzag across the steep direction and builds up speed along the flat one. The paper studies the family of two-step methods built on this idea, which differ in where they evaluate the gradient.

Definition · the family 𝓜

Given a step h > 0, momentum β ∈ [0, 1) and extrapolation τ ≥ 0, the method computes

Eq. 1

In words: take the last step again, scaled by β, and correct it with a gradient measured at a point τ steps further along the current direction of motion. The paper starts every trajectory from rest, x−1 = x0.

Three famous methods are members. Polyak's heavy ball has τ = 0, so it measures the gradient where it stands. Nesterov's accelerated method has τ = β, so it measures the gradient where momentum is about to carry it. The triple momentum method (TMM) of Van Scoy, Freeman and Lynch has τ approaching 1/2 as κ grows. Polyak's tuning for heavy ball is

Theorem 2.7

On the κ = 9 valley, √κ = 3, so β = (2/4)2 = 1/4 and h = 4/(3 + 1)2 = 1/4. The TMM tuning at κ = 9 (from Eq. 52 with design rate ϱ = 1 − κ−1/2 = 2/3) works out to hL = 5/3, β = 1/3 and τ = 1/5; that arithmetic is ours.

To see why the rate improves, treat each coordinate of a quadratic separately, exactly as for gradient descent. On a coordinate with curvature λ, Eq. 1 becomes a linear recurrence with two terms of memory, and its solutions are combinations of powers zk where z solves the characteristic equation

Section 2.1

derivationWhere does this polynomial come from?

This short check is ours. With ∇f(x) = λx on one coordinate, the update reads xk+1 = xk + β(xk − xk−1) − hλ[(1 + τ)xk − τxk−1]. Substituting xk = zk and dividing by zk−1 gives z2 = z + β(z − 1) − hλ[(1 + τ)z − τ]. Moving everything to one side,

Every solution of the recurrence is a combination of the two roots raised to the power k (or k zk at a double root), so the slower root decides the rate on that coordinate.

∎

For Polyak's tuning on the valley, the flat coordinate (λ = 1) gives χ1(z) = (z − 1)(z − 1/4) + z/4 = z2 − z + 1/4 = (z − 1/2)2, and the steep one (λ = 9) gives χ9(z) = (z − 1)(z − 1/4) + 9z/4 = (z + 1/2)2. Both have a double root of size 1/2, so every coordinate decays like k(1/2)k. That is the rate 1/2 per step against gradient descent's 0.8, and one millionth is reached in roughly 25 steps instead of 62.

The animation runs the three methods on the κ = 9 valley from the same start, (3, 0.8), at rest. Each frame is one step. The ellipses are level curves of f, and the bars underneath show each method's distance to the minimum on a log scale, so a constant rate shows up as bars shrinking by equal amounts.

Animation · three methods on the κ = 9 valley
gradient descentheavy ball (Polyak)TMM

A method is useless if some coordinate blows up, so the first question about any tuning is whether all roots of χλ lie inside the unit circle for every λ between μ and L. The paper calls such a tuning stable and gives a one-line test.

Fact · Lemma 2.1

A tuning of 𝓜 is stable if and only if y(1 + 2τ) < 2(1 + β), where y = hL.

proofWhy does stability reduce to one inequality?

A real quadratic z2 − Pz + Q has both roots strictly inside the unit circle exactly when |Q| < 1, 1 + Q − P > 0 and 1 + Q + P > 0 (the Schur–Cohn or Jury conditions). For χλ, P = 1 + β − hλ(1 + τ) and Q = β − hλτ ≤ β < 1.

The second condition is 1 + Q − P = χλ(1) = hλ > 0, which always holds. The third is 1 + Q + P = χλ(−1) = 2(1 + β) − hλ(1 + 2τ). It decreases in λ, so it holds for all λ ∈ [μ, L] exactly when it holds at λ = L, which is y(1 + 2τ) < 2(1 + β). Under that inequality also hλτ ≤ yτ < 1 + β, so Q > −1, completing |Q| < 1.

∎

For Polyak on the valley, y = 9/4 and τ = 0, so the test reads 9/4 < 2(5/4) = 5/2, which holds. For TMM, y(1 + 2τ) = (5/3)(7/5) = 7/3 < 2(4/3) = 8/3, which holds too.

In short: momentum turns each coordinate into a two-term recurrence with characteristic polynomial χλ; Polyak's tuning gives double roots of size 1/2 on the valley, and stability is the single inequality y(1 + 2τ) < 2(1 + β).

3 · RATES ON QUADRATICS AND BEYOND

What does it cost to look ahead?

Polyak's rate is the best possible on quadratics, so extrapolation can only make quadratics slower. The paper puts an exact price on it, and then defines the harder target: the worst rate over every function in the class, not just quadratics.

Definition · the quadratic rate and the worst-case rate

The quadratic rate is ρq = max over λ ∈ [μ, L] of the largest root modulus of χλ. The worst-case rate ρ𝓕 is defined through the envelope Γ(n) = sup ‖Sk+n‖/‖Sk‖, where Sk = (xk−1 − x⋆, xk − x⋆) is the state and the supremum runs over all real Hilbert spaces, all f ∈ 𝓕μ,L and all trajectories; then ρ𝓕 = lim Γ(n)1/n.

In words: ρq is the slowest per-step shrinkage on any quadratic bowl, and ρ𝓕 is the slowest long-run shrinkage an adversary can force by choosing any bowl at all, of any dimension.

Definition 2.2

Quadratics are in the class, so the adversary can always do at least as badly as on quadratics: ρ𝓕 ≥ ρq (Lemma 2.3). The interesting question is when the inequality is strict. The first result concerns ρq alone.

Theorem 2.7 · price of extrapolation

Equality holds exactly at Polyak's tuning. So extrapolating by τ is at least as bad, on quadratics, as running the optimal heavy ball on a problem whose condition number is inflated by roughly the factor 1 + 2τ.

proofWhy can no tuning beat this bound on quadratics?

Let ρ = ρq, let w1, w2 be the roots of χμ and v1, v2 those of χL, all of modulus at most ρ. Evaluating the factored polynomials at ±1,

where for complex conjugate roots one uses |1 − w|2 ≥ (1 − |w|)2. Also the product of the roots of χμ is β − hμτ = w1w2 ≤ ρ2.

Since χL(−1) = 2(1 + β) − hL(1 + 2τ), the second inequality gives hL(1 + 2τ) ≤ 2(1 + β) − (1 − ρ)2, and using β ≤ ρ2 + hμτ this is at most (1 + ρ)2 + 2hμτ. Dividing by hμ ≥ (1 − ρ)2,

which rearranges to the claim. Equality forces equality at every step: double roots w1 = w2 = ρ and v1 = v2 = −ρ, hence β − hμτ = ρ2 = β − hLτ, so τ = 0, and then β = ρ2, hμ = (1 − ρ)2, hL = (1 + ρ)2, which is Polyak's tuning.

∎

On the valley with TMM's τ = 1/5, κτ = 1.4 · 9 − 0.4 = 12.2 and the bound is (√12.2 − 1)/(√12.2 + 1) ≈ 0.555. TMM's actual quadratic rate is 2/3 (its χμ factors as (z − 2/3)(z − 4/9), Theorem F.1), comfortably above the bound. For the standard Nesterov tuning at κ = 9 (h = 1/9, τ = β = 1/2), κτ = 17 and the bound is ≈ 0.610; we computed its quadratic rate numerically as 2/3. Both pay for looking ahead, compared with Polyak's 1/2.

Fact

On quadratics, heavy ball is the champion and every bit of extrapolation is a cost. The rest of the paper explains why methods pay this cost anyway: on non-quadratic functions, heavy ball's advantage can turn into failure.

In short: ρ𝓕 ≥ ρq ≥ (√κτ − 1)/(√κτ + 1), with equality only for Polyak's heavy ball.

4 · THE SLOW FLOW

What equation does an accelerated method approximate?

When κ is large, accelerated methods take tiny, careful steps along the flat direction, and many steps together look like a smooth motion. Identifying that motion turns questions about rates into questions about a damped oscillator, which can be solved exactly.

Definition · accelerated scaling and slow data

Normalize L = 1, so μ = ε2 = 1/κ. A family of tunings is in accelerated scaling with slow data (θ, y) when

Eq. 3

In words: the momentum falls short of 1 by θ/√κ, and the step times L tends to y.

Each method in Section 2 has slow data. For Polyak, 1 − β ≈ 4/√κ and hL = 4κ/(√κ + 1)2 → 4, so (θ, y) = (4, 4). For standard Nesterov, (θ, y, τ) → (2, 1, 1) (Corollary 6.6). For TMM, (θ, y, τ) → (3, 2, 1/2) (Corollary 7.1). The Polyak computation is ours.

Rescaling time as t = εk, the paper states that the iterates follow the heavy-ball equation

Section 3

derivationWhy does a discrete method turn into this differential equation?

This heuristic is ours; the paper states the limit and proves its consequences rigorously by other means. Write xk = X(εk) for a smooth curve X and ignore the small extrapolation shift. Rearranging Eq. 1,

By Taylor expansion the second difference is about ε2Ẍ and the first difference about εẊ, while 1 − β = θε. The left side is therefore about ε2(Ẍ + θẊ), and the right side is about −y∇f(X). Dividing by ε2 gives Ẍ + θẊ + (y/ε2)∇f(X) = 0. The function F = (y/ε2)f has curvatures between y and yκ, which explains the class in the display.

∎

On a quadratic bowl in the flat direction, F = (y/2)x2, the equation is ẍ + θẋ + yx = 0. Trying x = e−ζt gives ζ2 − θζ + y = 0. If the roots are complex the solution oscillates and decays at rate θ/2; if real, the slower root ζ− wins. Time t corresponds to t/ε = t√κ steps, so decay e−ct is a per-step factor e−c/√κ ≈ 1 − c/√κ. The paper's quadratic constant is

Eq. 4

and Lemma 2.5 shows that √κ(1 − ρq) never exceeds cQ in the limit, and tends to cQ when y(1 + 2τ) < 4. The constant is largest at critical damping θ = 2√y, where cQ = √y.

Check this on the running oscillators. For (θ, m) = (2, 1), θ2 = 4 = 4m is critical damping, cQ = 1, and the solutions are (A + Bt)e−t. For (3, 2), ζ2 − 3ζ + 2 = (ζ − 1)(ζ − 2), so cQ = 1 again. For Polyak's (4, 4), critical damping gives cQ = 2, matching (√κ − 1)/(√κ + 1) ≈ 1 − 2/√κ. On quadratics, then, Nesterov and TMM both have constant 1 and Polyak has 2.

Fact

Methods with the same slow data (θ, y) discretize the same oscillator, and on quadratics they share the constant cQ(θ, y). The paper's point is that on general functions they need not share anything.

In short: with β = 1 − θ/√κ and hL → y, a momentum method becomes the oscillator ẍ + θẋ + ∇F = 0, and on quadratics it gains the factor 1 − cQ/√κ per step.

5 · THE OSCILLATOR ON GENERAL FUNCTIONS

Where does θ/3 come from?

The oscillator is linear only on quadratics. On a general strongly convex F the restoring force ∇F is nonlinear, and an adversary can shape it to keep the ball circling. Theorem 3.1 finds the exact slowest decay, and it is often worse than cQ.

Write the function as f(x) = (m/2)‖x‖2 + fm(x), where the remainder fm is convex with fm(0) = 0 and ∇fm(0) = 0. Convexity between x and the minimizer gives two inequalities that are the only information the argument uses,

Eq. 6

The tool is an energy that must decrease. For a trial rate c, put Δc = c2 − θc + m and

Theorem 3.1(a)

Along every solution of ẍ + θẋ + ∇f(x) = 0 it satisfies the exact identity

Eq. 9

proofHow does the derivative come out so cleanly?

The paper's proof, with the algebra filled in. Put v = ẋ, G = ∇fm(x) and a = θ − c. The equation of motion is v̇ = −θv − mx − G, so v̇ + av = −cv − mx − G. Differentiating the three terms of Vc,

The terms ⟨G, v⟩ and −⟨v, G⟩ cancel. Now add 2cVc = 2cfm + cΔc‖x‖2 + c‖v + ax‖2 and collect. The ‖v‖2 terms are −c + c = 0. The ⟨x, v⟩ terms are Δc − m − ac + 2ac = Δc − m + ac = 0, because Δc = m − ca. The ‖x‖2 terms are −am + cΔc + ca2 = −am + cm − c2a + ca2 = −(a − c)(m − ca) = −(θ − 2c)Δc. What remains is 2cfm − a⟨G, x⟩, which equals −(θ − c)(⟨G, x⟩ − fm) − (θ − 3c)fm. Multiplying V̇c + 2cVc by e2ct gives Eq. 9.

When 0 < c ≤ θ/3 and Δc > 0, all three coefficients θ − 2c, θ − c, θ − 3c are nonnegative, and Eq. 6 makes every bracketed term nonnegative. So e2ctVc never increases, Vc ≤ e−2ctVc(0), and since Vc controls ‖x‖2 + ‖ẋ‖2 from above and below, the state decays at rate c.

∎

The three coefficients explain everything. The middle and last ones need c ≤ θ − c and c ≤ θ/3, and the first needs Δc > 0, which (with c < θ/2) is exactly c < cQ (Lemma B.1). The binding one on general functions is θ − 3c. The paper gives the reason it is 3: if the remainder were homogeneous of degree r, so that ⟨∇fm(x), x⟩ = rfm(x), the fm terms in the bracket would combine to (rθ − (r + 2)c)fm, which vanishes at c = rθ/(r + 2). Quadratic profiles (r = 2) give θ/2. Cone-shaped profiles (r = 1), the flattest growth convexity allows, give θ/3.

Definition · the full-class constant

Eq. 5

In words: the oscillator decays at least as fast as the slower of the cone rate θ/3 and the quadratic rate cQ.

The energy argument shows that every solution decays at least at rate c𝓕. The converse needs a function on which the ball decays no faster. Theorem 3.1(c) builds one for every rate between θ/3 and cQ: a trajectory that is an orthogonal sum of J planar spirals, x(t) = (√νj e(−c + iγj)t)j, each turning at its own angular speed γj and shrinking at exactly rate c, together with a smooth strongly convex function whose gradient flow produces it. A single spiral does not work (Proposition 3.3): near c = θ/3 it would have to wind so fast that convexity fails at its first return to the starting ray. Mixing spirals with different speeds desynchronizes those returns.

Fact · Theorem 3.1(d)

Over all strongly convex functions with curvature at least m and all nonzero solutions, the slowest decay exponent of the heavy-ball flow is exactly c𝓕(θ, m) = min(θ/3, cQ(θ, m)).

On the running oscillators: for (2, 1), cQ = 1 but θ/3 = 2/3, so c𝓕 = 2/3. Nesterov's slow flow loses a third of its quadratic speed on general functions. For (3, 2), θ/3 = 1 = cQ, so c𝓕 = 1 and nothing is lost. The extra friction in TMM's flow is exactly what balances the two constraints.

Fact · Corollary 3.2

For fixed m, the best quadratic exponent is √m, at θ = 2√m, and the best full-class exponent is √(m/2), at θ = 3√(m/2), where θ/3 = cQ. Optimizing for all functions costs a factor 1/√2 in speed and needs about 1.06 times as much friction.

proofWhy is the full-class maximum at the crossing point?

For θ ≤ 2√m, cQ = θ/2 and c𝓕 = θ/3 ≤ (2/3)√m, which is below √(m/2). For θ ≥ 2√m, cQ = ζ− = 2m/(θ + √(θ2 − 4m)) decreases from √m while θ/3 increases, so the minimum of the two is largest where they meet. They meet when ζ = θ/3 solves ζ2 − θζ + m = 0, that is θ2/9 − θ2/3 + m = 0, so θ = 3√(m/2) and the common value is √(m/2).

∎

In short: an energy identity with coefficient θ − 3c caps the oscillator at θ/3 on general functions, spiral mixtures show the cap is real, and the exact exponent is c𝓕 = min(θ/3, cQ).

6 · THE HALF-STEP WALL

Why does heavy ball fail where Nesterov succeeds?

Heavy ball and Nesterov's method can share slow data, hence the same oscillator, yet heavy ball is not accelerated on 𝓕μ,L. The flow cannot see the difference, so it must come from the discretization. The paper locates it in a phase shift of exactly half a step.

Think of a slowly rotating trajectory, one that turns by an angle ω per step, written as xk = eiωk in a plane. A derivative multiplies such a wave by iω. A difference multiplies it by something slightly different, and the paper writes the discrepancy as

Eq. 23

derivationWhy is the extra phase exactly ω/2?

Factor out the midpoint: 1 − eiω = eiω/2(e−iω/2 − eiω/2) = eiω/2 · (−2i sin(ω/2)). Writing −2i sin(ω/2) = (2 sin(ω/2)/ω)(−iω) gives Eq. 23. The real factor 2 sin(ω/2)/ω is close to 1 for small ω, so the only real distortion is the phase eiω/2: a one-step difference acts like a derivative taken at the midpoint, half a step away.

∎

The energy argument of Section 5 uses the convexity inequalities at matching times. In discrete time the gradient is sampled at query points, and the half-step lag from Eq. 23 has to be compensated by the query being far enough ahead. The paper measures how far ahead with a phase.

Definition · the spectral phase lead

For the limit method (μ = 0, L = 1, β = 1) of a tuning in 𝓜 with slow step y and extrapolation τ, the phase at frequency ω is

Section 5.3

and Θ0(ω)/ω is the phase lead, measured in steps. In words: it says how many steps ahead of the iterate the gradient effectively looks, for a component that rotates by ω per step.

For small ω, ξ ≈ ω2/2 and sin ω ≈ ω, so Θ0(ω) ≈ yτω/y = τω: at low frequencies the lead is τ steps. Remark 5.7 records the two extremes: for the limit of standard Nesterov, (y, τ) = (1, 1), the lead is exactly 1 at every frequency; for TMM, (y, τ) = (2, 1/2), it is exactly 1/2 at every frequency in (0, π).

The lead matters because of a resonance test. A one-atom spectrum at ω = 2π/K, which corresponds to a trajectory rotating once every K steps, is feasible at zero decay exactly when |Θ(2π/K)| ≤ π/K, that is, when the lead at that frequency is at most 1/2 step (Lemma C.14). Feasible means a function exists on which the method rotates forever without converging (Proposition 4.10). So the curve Θ0(ω)/ω must stay above the half-step line at the frequencies 2π/K, or the method has periodic orbits.

The animation computes Θ0(ω)/ω for five limit methods and marks every K from 3 to 40 at which the curve passes strictly below the half-step line, which is where periodic witnesses appear. The tuning (y, τ) = (1, 1/4) reproduces the paper's Figure 3, where strict passage starts at K = 8.

Animation · phase lead against the half-step line

The same information appears algebraically in the lag-one polynomial. The paper shows (Proposition 6.1) that the quantity Re[(1 − eiω)χμ(eiω)conj(χL(eiω))] equals ξ times a quadratic Lτ(ξ), that Θ(ω) > ω/2 exactly when Lτ(ξ) > 0, and that positivity of Lτ on (0, 2] certifies convergence. In the limit β = 1, μ = 0,

Proposition 6.1(a)

Near ξ = 0 the linear term dominates, and its sign is the sign of 2τ − 1. With τ < 1/2 the polynomial is negative at small ξ, which means at slowly rotating frequencies 2π/K for large K. On the valley, plugging TMM's limiting y = 2, τ = 1/2 gives Lτ ≡ 0: TMM sits exactly on the wall, tight at every frequency at once.

Fact · Theorem 6.2, the wall τ = 1/2

If stable tunings are accelerated on quadratics and lim sup τκ < 1/2, then for all large κ there is an integer K ≥ 6 with Θ(2π/K) < π/K, the method has trajectories that approach K-periodic orbits in ℝ3, and it does not converge uniformly on 𝓕μ,L. Consequently every family accelerated on 𝓕μ,L has lim inf τκ ≥ 1/2.

proof sketchHow does a negative coefficient become a periodic orbit?

If the claim failed, Lemma E.4 provides a subsequence of tunings with β → 1, hμ → 0, yε → y > 0 and τε → τ < 1/2. Along it the lag-one polynomials converge coefficient by coefficient to L0(ξ) = 2y(2τ − 1)ξ + 4(1 − τy)ξ2. The negative linear coefficient makes L0 negative on some interval (0, ξ0). Choose an integer K ≥ 6 with 1 − cos(2π/K) < ξ0; by convergence the actual polynomials are negative there for all small ε. Proposition 6.1 converts this into Θ(2π/K) < π/K, and Proposition 4.10 builds a function in 𝓕μ,L(ℝ3) on which the iterates approach a K-periodic rotation. Such a trajectory never converges, contradicting acceleration.

∎

In particular, every heavy-ball tuning that accelerates on quadratics has periodic orbits on 𝓕μ,L once κ is large. The paper proves this abstractly. To see it happen, the animation below runs a concrete example of our own: the one-dimensional function whose derivative is 25x for x < 1, x + 24 for 1 ≤ x < 2, and 25x − 24 for x ≥ 2. Its derivative is continuous and increasing with slopes between 1 and 25, so it lies in 𝓕1,25 with κ = 25 and minimizer 0. We run Polyak's heavy ball (β = 4/9, h = 1/9, optimal on quadratics with rate 2/3) and TMM at κ = 25 (ϱ = 0.8, hL = 1.8, β = 8/15, τ = 8/27 from Eq. 52) from x0 = 3.3 at rest.

The function and both runs are ours. They illustrate Theorem 6.2 and Theorem 8.1(b) for one κ; the paper's own witnesses are built differently, in ℝ3. The heavy-ball iterates settle onto the 3-cycle −1.802, 2.116, 0.647.

In short: a difference lags a derivative by half a step, so a method whose gradient looks less than half a step ahead resonates with slowly rotating trajectories; acceleration on all of 𝓕μ,L forces τ ≥ 1/2 in the limit.

7 · THE EXACT CONSTANT AND THE BEST TUNINGS

How fast is each method, exactly?

With the flow ceiling and the wall in hand, the main theorem says that beyond the wall nothing else is lost: the discrete method is exactly as fast as its oscillator on the worst function.

Fact · Theorem 2.6

For a family of stable tunings in accelerated scaling: (a) for every τ ≥ 0 there are functions in fixed finite dimension on which the iterates from rest decay no faster than e−(c𝓕 + δ)εN; (b) if τ > 1/2 and y(1 + 2τ) < 4, the rate is better than 1 − cε for every c < c𝓕, certified by the lag-one criterion. Hence, under (b),

Theorem 5.2 extends the ceiling to every second-order method with the same slow data and any fixed finite memory, not only two-step methods. The theorem also hands a recipe for designing a target constant c: the paper notes that c𝓕(θ, y) ≥ c is equivalent to θ ≥ 3c and y ≥ cθ − c2. The smallest step is then y = 2c2 at θ = 3c, and the stability-type condition y(1 + 2τ) ≤ 4 caps the constant at √(2/(1 + 2τ)) for fixed τ (Corollary E.11).

Apply the recipe to the Nesterov family, where τ = β → 1: the cap is √(2/3). Corollary 6.7 shows it is attained by h = 4/(3L), τ = β = 1 − √(6/κ), whose slow data θ = √6, y = 4/3 satisfy θ = 3c and y = 2c2 with c = √(2/3). At τ → 1/2 the cap is 1, which is TMM.

Nesterov tuningθyFull-class constant c
Standard212/3
Quadratic-optimal4/√34/34/(3√3) ≈ 0.770
Class-optimal asymptotically√64/3√(2/3) ≈ 0.816

Table 2 · Corollaries 6.6 and 6.7

The standard constant 2/3 is the running oscillator (2, 1) from Section 5: θ/3 = 2/3 beats cQ = 1, and since τ = 1 > 1/2 and y(1 + 2τ) = 3 < 4, Theorem 2.6 applies directly. This recovers the constant found earlier by Gannot and by Pokutta and Stellato. For squared distances every constant doubles, so standard Nesterov contracts squared distance by 1 − (4/3)κ−1/2 per step.

The optimum over the whole family is c = 1. Corollary E.11(v) shows it forces (θ, y, τ) → (3, 2, 1/2), the second running oscillator, which the paper calls the TMM corner. TMM itself has ρ𝓕 = ρq = 1 − κ−1/2 exactly at every κ (Corollary 7.1; the upper bound is due to Van Scoy, Freeman and Lynch), which is 2/3 on the valley, and this rate is optimal among all deterministic first-order methods by Drori and Taylor. Its parameters approach the corner from below the wall, with 1/2 − τ = (5/4)κ−1/2(1 + O(κ−1/2)), so for every finite κ it looks slightly less than half a step ahead.

The paper then classifies every way to reach constant 1. Writing τ = 1/2 − aε and hL = 2 − bε near the corner (Eq. 28), Theorem 7.2(d) says the constant is 1 exactly when θ = 3, a ≤ 5/4 and 2a + b ≥ 7/2. That is a wedge in the (a, b) plane, and TMM, with (a, b) = (5/4, 1), is its vertex. Theorem 7.5 extends the classification to arbitrary rates of approach.

Fact · Theorem 5.8 and Corollary 5.9

For any fixed finite memory, if the limiting lag-one symbol is nonnegative at every frequency, then y ≤ 2, the full-class constant is at most 1 and the quadratic constant at most √2, which is 1/√2 times Polyak's 2. Equality y = 2 holds only for the limiting transfer function of TMM, −(z − 1)2/(3z − 1).

The proof of Theorem 5.8 is a trace formula: 2/y − 1 equals an integral over frequencies of the lag-one symbol against a positive weight (Eq. 24), so a nonnegative symbol forces 2/y − 1 ≥ 0, and a symbol that vanishes identically forces the transfer function by an analyticity argument.

Finally, Section 8 leaves asymptotics behind. Theorem 8.1 says that at fixed (β, τ), every stable choice of h, μ and L converges if and only if τ ≥ τ3(β) = (β2 + 3β − 1)/6; below that threshold some stable choice has 3-periodic orbits. For heavy ball, τ = 0, this means every stable tuning converges at every condition number exactly when β ≤ (√13 − 3)/2 ≈ 0.303. Polyak's tuning on the κ = 9 valley has β = 1/4, under the threshold, so it converges on every function in 𝓕1,9. At κ = 25 its β = 4/9 is over the threshold, consistent with the 3-cycle in the last animation. Every stable tuning of the Nesterov family τ = β converges, whatever h, μ and L.

In short: beyond the wall the rate is exactly the flow's min(θ/3, cQ), which gives 2/3 for standard Nesterov, √(2/3) for its best tuning and 1 only at the TMM corner (θ, y, τ) = (3, 2, 1/2).

What the paper proves, in numbers

In short: one formula, min(θ/3, cQ), plus one wall, τ ≥ 1/2, organizes the exact asymptotic rates of the whole two-step family.

9 · ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what isn't

What is shown is a complete picture for two-step methods in the large-κ limit. Upper bounds come from explicit certificates (nonnegative combinations of interpolation inequalities) and lower bounds from explicit functions built from spirals or periodic rotations, so the constants are exact rather than merely bounded. Several known constants are recovered (Nesterov's 2/3, TMM's 1) and some improved; for HNAG++ the squared-distance coefficient 4√2/3 improves the global coefficient √2 of its authors. The finite-κ threshold of Theorem 8.1 is exact and clean. Our own checks agree with the paper on every point we tested: Polyak's rate 1/2 and TMM's 2/3 on the valley, TMM's factorization of χμ and χL, the identity (9), and the Figure 3 claim that strict passage for (y, τ) = (1, 1/4) starts at K = 8.

The limits are mostly of scope. Almost all constants are asymptotic: o(κ−1/2) errors are not quantified, so the theorems do not say how large κ must be before, for example, Nesterov's worst case really is 1 − (2/3)κ−1/2. The exceptions are TMM's exact rate and the thresholds of Section 8. The rates are worst cases over the entire class, achieved by carefully built functions whose dimension can grow as the target precision improves; they say nothing about typical problems, and the paper does not claim they do. Some cases remain open: the arithmetic gap at the corner, whether accelerated methods with three or more steps of memory must have a nonnegative symbol at every frequency, the size of the worst-case dimension, and periodic or time-varying methods.

The paper states that all results have formal proofs in the Lean proof assistant, with a public repository; we did not inspect it. It also states that the authors used AI tools to assist with exposition, formal proof verification and literature checks, and that they verified the statements and take responsibility for them. It is a fresh preprint and has not been refereed.

A connection, oursMachine learning optimizers such as quasi-hyperbolic momentum are members of 𝓜 (Remark 4.4 gives the dictionary τ = (1 − ν)β/(1 − β)). The paper's Corollary 6.6(iii) implies that a fixed weight ν < 1 with β → 1 cannot accelerate even on quadratics, which is a precise version of the folklore that these optimizers behave like plain gradient descent unless tuned in a very particular way. The paper states the corollary; the folklore reading is ours.

In short: exact, certified and formalized for two-step methods as κ → ∞; asymptotic and worst-case by design, with a few precisely stated gaps.

FURTHER READING

Background the paper builds on, not opened from here and listed without links: Polyak, "Some methods of speeding up the convergence of iteration methods" (1964); Nesterov, Lectures on Convex Optimization (2018); Lessard, Recht and Packard, "Analysis and design of optimization algorithms via integral quadratic constraints" (SIAM J. Optim., 2016); Van Scoy, Freeman and Lynch, "The fastest known globally convergent first-order method for minimizing strongly convex functions" (2018); Goujaud, Taylor and Dieuleveut, "Provable non-accelerations of the heavy-ball method" (Math. Program., 2025); Drori and Taylor, "On the oracle complexity of smooth strongly convex minimization" (J. Complexity, 2022).

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.13584v1. Equation, lemma and theorem numbers match the paper. All three animations run real computations: the three methods on the κ = 9 quadratic, the phase lead Θ0(ω)/ω from the paper's formula with resonant K found by direct evaluation, and the two methods on a piecewise quadratic. The gradient-descent background, the derivation of χλ, the slow-flow heuristic, Polyak's slow data, the κ = 9 and κ = 25 tunings, the piecewise example and the numerical check of Nesterov's quadratic rate at κ = 9 are ours.

Entropy Maximization for Cube Projections

Zhekai Pang · posted Nov 10, 2026 · math.PR · arXiv 2611.13533

Overview

Shine a light through a cube onto a line and the shadow of a uniformly random point is a weighted sum of independent uniform numbers; this paper proves that, in every dimension n ≥ 150, the shadow is most spread out, in the sense of Shannon's differential entropy, exactly when all the weights have the same size. The question was posed by Eskenazis, Nayar and Tkocz, and the proof has two halves of very different flavor. The first is a clean averaging argument that reduces the whole theorem to one sign: the third derivative of the logarithm of a single density must be negative. The second proves that sign with a trick from statistics called exponential tilting, which moves every point to the center of a reweighted distribution, followed by careful Fourier estimates in which a Gaussian approximation is made rigorous with explicit constants. The constants are what force the restriction n ≥ 150.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • why every projection Σ aiUi with Σ ai2 = 1 has the same variance 1/3, and what differential entropy measures beyond the variance;
  • why the Gaussian has the most entropy for a given variance, and the one-line inequality behind it, which the paper reuses;
  • the "Robin Hood" step that replaces two weights by their root mean square, and why it raises the expectation of any even function whose third derivative is positive on the right;
  • how repeating that step drives every weight to 1/√n, and why the theorem then reduces to the sign condition (log qn)‴ ≤ 0;
  • exponential tilting: how reweighting a uniform variable by etu moves any point of the support to the mean, so a sign at every point becomes a sign at the origin;
  • how the derivatives of a density at 0 are integrals of its characteristic function, why the skewness E[Y3] must be kept as a factor, and where the number 150 comes from.
notationSymbols used throughout
U, Ui

a = (a1, …, an)
a unit vector of weights, Σ ai2 = 1; the projection is X = Σ aiUi

differential entropy, −∫ f log f, where f is the density of X; log is the natural logarithm
pn, qn
the densities of U1 + ⋯ + Un and of the equal-weight projection n−1/2(U1 + ⋯ + Un)
V
V = −log qn, so that E[V(X)] is a cross-entropy
K(t)
the cumulant generating function of U, K(t) = log E[etU] = log(sinh t / t)

the tilted uniform, with density ½etu − K(t) on [−1, 1], and its standardized version Y = (Ut − E[Ut])/√Var(Ut)

W = n−1/2(Y1 + ⋯ + Yn) for independent copies of Y, and its density w

Two running examples
  • Two coins. The projection X = aU1 + bU2 with a2 + b2 = 1 and a ≥ b ≥ 0, at three settings: (1, 0), (0.8, 0.6) and (1/√2, 1/√2). The densities are a box, a trapezoid and a triangle, every quantity in the chapter can be computed by hand, and the entropies come out as 0.6931, 0.8450 and 0.8466.
  • Four coins. The weights a = (3, 2, 1, 1)/√15, so the squared weights are (0.6, 0.2667, 0.0667, 0.0667). This is the starting point for the averaging process of Section 4, which reaches the equal weights (1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2) in six steps.
1 · PROJECTIONS OF A CUBE

What is a cube projection?

Pick a point uniformly at random from the cube [−1, 1]n. Its coordinates are independent and each is uniform on [−1, 1]. Now choose a direction, a unit vector a, and record only the component of the point along that direction. That number is the shadow of the random point on the line through a, and the question of the paper is which direction makes the shadow most random.

Definition · cube projection

For a ∈ ℝn with Σ ai2 = 1, the one-dimensional projection of the uniform distribution on the cube in direction a is the law of the random variable X = Σi aiUi, where U1, …, Un are independent and uniform on [−1, 1].

In words: a weighted sum of independent uniform numbers, with weights whose squares add to one.

The normalization makes all directions comparable in the crudest sense. A uniform variable on [−1, 1] has mean 0 and variance ∫−11 u2/2 du = 1/3, and variances of independent variables add, so

Section 1

Every shadow has variance 1/3, whatever the direction. The shapes still differ a great deal, and the two-coin example shows how. With a = (1, 0) the shadow is U1 itself, a flat box of height 1/2 on [−1, 1]. With a = (1/√2, 1/√2) it is a triangle on [−√2, √2] with peak 1/√2, because the sum of two independent uniforms piles up in the middle. In between, with a = (0.8, 0.6), the density is a trapezoid: flat at height 1/(2a) = 0.625 on [−0.2, 0.2] and falling linearly to zero at ±1.4.

derivationWhy is the density of aU1 + bU2 a trapezoid?

The paper writes this density as Eq. 3. Condition on U2: given bU2 = y, the sum is uniform on [y − a, y + a] with density 1/(2a). Averaging over y, which is uniform on [−b, b], the density at x is 1/(2a) times the probability that |x − bU2| ≤ a. For 0 ≤ x ≤ a − b this probability is 1, for a − b < x < a + b it is (a + b − x)/(2b), and beyond a + b it is 0. Multiplying by 1/(2a) gives

and the density is even. When a = b the flat part disappears and the trapezoid becomes the triangle (2c − x)/(4c2) with c = a.

∎

A different measure of size already has a famous answer. The value of the density at 0 is, up to the factor 2−n, the area of the slice of the cube through its center perpendicular to a. Ball's cube slicing theorem, cited by the paper, says this is largest at a = (1, 1, 0, …, 0)/√2, with two nonzero coordinates. So "largest central slice" picks a very unbalanced direction. Entropy is a different functional, and the conjecture is that it prefers the most balanced one.

In short: a cube projection is X = Σ aiUi with Σ ai2 = 1; all have variance 1/3, and the two-coin example gives a box, a trapezoid and a triangle.

2 · DIFFERENTIAL ENTROPY

How do we measure spread beyond the variance?

Variance cannot tell the shadows apart, so a finer measure is needed. Shannon's differential entropy measures how evenly a density spreads its mass: roughly, eh is the length of an interval on which a uniform variable would be equally unpredictable.

Definition · differential entropy

Theorem 1.1

In words: the average of −log f over the distribution itself. Places where the density is small contribute large values of −log f, so a density that spreads its mass thinly over a wide range has large entropy.

For the box of height 1/2 on [−1, 1], −log f = log 2 everywhere, so h = log 2 ≈ 0.6931. For a uniform variable on an interval of length ℓ the same calculation gives log ℓ, which is the sense in which eh is an effective width. The triangle and the trapezoid need a short integration, and the result for the whole two-coin family fits on one line.

Fact · two coins, our computation

For a ≥ b ≥ 0, the projection aU1 + bU2 has entropy log(2a) + b/(2a). At (1, 0) this is log 2 ≈ 0.6931; at (0.8, 0.6) it is log 1.6 + 0.375 ≈ 0.8450; at (1/√2, 1/√2) it is log √2 + 1/2 ≈ 0.8466.

derivationWhere does log(2a) + b/(2a) come from, and why is it largest at a = b?

This derivation is ours; the paper does not treat n = 2 separately. Write p = 1/(2a) for the plateau height. The plateau has total width 2(a − b) and contributes −2(a − b)p log p. Each of the two ramps has width 2b and runs linearly from p down to 0; substituting f for x, its contribution is (2b/p)∫0p(−f log f) df = 2b(p/4 − (p/2)log p). Adding,

using 2ap = 1. On the unit circle put a = cos φ and b = sin φ with 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/4. Then h(φ) = log(2 cos φ) + (tan φ)/2, and

So the entropy rises all the way from φ = 0 to φ = π/4, where a = b. For two coins the conjecture is therefore true, by a calculation the paper's method does not need.

∎

There is a ceiling that every shadow must respect. Among all densities with a given variance σ2, the Gaussian has the most entropy, namely ½ log(2πeσ2). For σ2 = 1/3 that ceiling is ½ log(2πe/3) ≈ 0.8696. The triangle at 0.8466 is already close to it, and the equal-weight four-coin shadow, at 0.8667 by our numerical computation, is closer still.

proofWhy can nothing beat the Gaussian, and what inequality does that use?

This is standard background, and the same inequality is the last step of the paper's Proposition 2.2. For u ≥ 0, u log u − u + 1 ≥ 0, with equality only at u = 1 (the left side is convex in u and has a minimum of 0 at u = 1). Let f and g be densities with g positive. Put u = f/g, multiply by g and integrate. The terms −f + g integrate to −1 + 1 = 0, so

That is, h(f) ≤ Ef[−log g] for any density g, with equality only when f = g. Take g Gaussian with variance σ2: −log g(x) = ½ log(2πσ2) + x2/(2σ2), and its average under any f with variance σ2 is ½ log(2πσ2) + ½ = ½ log(2πeσ2).

∎

The central limit theorem suggests why balance should help: a sum with many comparable terms looks more Gaussian than a sum dominated by one term, and the Gaussian is the entropy champion. That heuristic is ours, and it is only a heuristic, because for a fixed n there is no monotone path from "unbalanced" to "Gaussian" that obviously raises entropy. The paper notes two related facts in the literature: the entropy of the equal-weight sum n−1/2(U1 + ⋯ + Un) is nondecreasing in n (Artstein, Ball, Barthe and Naor), and it converges to the Gaussian value (Barron). The paper's question is about a fixed n.

Fact · Theorem 1.1

Let n ≥ 150. For every a ∈ ℝn with Σ ai2 = 1,

with equality if and only if |ai| = 1/√n for every i.

The same statement was already known for other summands. Eskenazis, Nayar and Tkocz proved it for Gaussian scale mixtures, and Bartczak, Nayar and Zwara for nonnegative weights on Gamma(α) summands when nα ≥ 1. The earlier Fourier criterion of Malliaris does not directly apply to the uniform case, because it assumes a positive Fourier transform and the characteristic function of U, sin t / t, changes sign.

In short: entropy h = E[−log f] separates shadows of equal variance; for two coins it equals log(2a) + b/(2a), which peaks at a = b, and the theorem says equal weights win for every n ≥ 150.

3 · THE ROBIN HOOD STEP

What happens when two weights are made equal?

The natural strategy is to balance the weights a little at a time. Take the two weights a1 ≥ a2 and replace both by their root mean square c = √((a12 + a22)/2), which keeps Σ ai2 = 1. Taking from the rich weight and giving to the poor one is why we call it a Robin Hood step; the idea goes back to Latała and Oleszkiewicz, whose averaging argument the paper adapts. The step does not obviously raise entropy, so the paper shows instead that it raises the expectation of a well-chosen function V.

Fact · Lemma 2.1

Let V be even and three times continuously differentiable on (−R, R) with V‴(x) ≥ 0 for 0 < x < R. Let Y be independent of U1, U2, and either Y = 0 or Y has an even unimodal density. If a ≥ b ≥ 0, c = √((a2 + b2)/2), and |Y| ≤ L with 2c + L < R, then

In words: smoothing out two weights can only increase the average of V, as long as V is symmetric and its third derivative is positive on the right. The rest of the sum, Y, is carried along unchanged. The proof is worth seeing because each step is elementary, and it has three moves.

First move: absorb Y. Let g(x) = E[V(x + Y)]. Then the two expectations are E[g(aU1 + bU2)] and E[g(cU1 + cU2)], so it is enough to compare g against two densities. The function g inherits the key property: it is even, and g‴ ≥ 0 on [0, 2c].

proofWhy does averaging V against Y keep the third derivative nonnegative?

Let q be the even unimodal density of Y. Differentiating under the expectation and substituting u = x + y, then splitting at 0 and using that V‴ is odd and q is even,

For x, u ≥ 0, |u − x| ≤ u + x, and q is nonincreasing in |·|, so the bracket is nonnegative, and the hypothesis V‴(u) ≥ 0 for u > 0 does the rest.

∎

Second move: change variable to x2. Define ψ(s) = g(√s). Because g is even with g′(0) = 0 and g″ is nondecreasing on [0, 2c], the paper shows xg″(x) − g′(x) ≥ 0 (Eq. 1), and then

Lemma 2.1, after Eq. 1

So g(x) = ψ(x2) is a convex function of x2. This is the only thing the rest of the argument uses about V.

proofWhy is xg″(x) − g′(x) nonnegative?

Since g′(0) = 0, g′(x) = ∫0x g″(v) dv, and xg″(x) = ∫0x g″(x) dv. Subtracting, xg″(x) − g′(x) = ∫0x[g″(x) − g″(v)] dv, and the integrand is nonnegative because g″ is nondecreasing (g‴ ≥ 0). The formula for ψ″ is the chain rule applied twice to g(√t).

∎

Third move: compare the two densities. Let f1 be the density of aU1 + bU2 (the trapezoid) and f2 that of c(U1 + U2) (the triangle). Both live on [−2c, 2c], both have total mass 1/2 on the right half-line, and both have the same second moment there, because the variances agree:

Eq. 2

Moreover f2 − f1 changes sign exactly twice on (0, 2c), with pattern +, −, +: the triangle is taller in the middle and reaches further out, and the trapezoid is fatter in between. Call the sign changes r1 < r2. Let ℓ be the straight line, in the variable s = x2, that agrees with ψ at s = r12 and s = r22. Convexity puts ψ below ℓ between the two points and above it outside, which is exactly where f2 − f1 is negative and positive. So (ψ(x2) − ℓ(x2))(f2 − f1)(x) ≥ 0 everywhere, and since ℓ(x2) is a constant plus a multiple of x2, Eq. 2 makes it integrate to zero against f2 − f1. Therefore

Eq. 4

Doubling for the left half-line gives E[g(cU1 + cU2)] − E[g(aU1 + bU2)] ≥ 0, which is the lemma.

proofWhy exactly two sign changes, in the order +, −, +?

From c < a and c2 > ab (both follow from a > b and the definition of c), Eq. 3 shows that f2 − f1 starts positive at x = 0 (f2(0) = 1/(2c) > 1/(2a) = f1(0)), strictly decreases on [0, a − b] (f1 is flat and f2 falls), strictly increases on [a − b, a + b] (f1 falls with slope 1/(4ab), faster than f2's 1/(4c2)), and is nonnegative on [a + b, 2c] where f1 = 0. Because it integrates to zero, it must be negative somewhere. A function that goes down and then up crosses zero at most twice, and here it must cross twice.

∎

On the two-coin example with (a, b) = (0.8, 0.6) everything can be checked. Here c = √0.5 ≈ 0.7071, so the triangle lives on [0, 1.4142] and the trapezoid on [0, 1.4]. At the origin, f2(0) = 0.7071 > f1(0) = 0.625. At x = 0.2, the end of the plateau, f2 − f1 ≈ −0.0179. At x = 1.4 the trapezoid is gone and f2 ≈ 0.0071 > 0. The two sign changes are at r1 ≈ 0.1642 and r2 ≈ 1.0589 (our numerical root-finding). Both halves have second moment (a2 + b2)/6 = 1/6, as the paper computes. And with V = −log, the conclusion of this section is visible in the entropies already found: 0.8450 for the trapezoid and 0.8466 for the triangle.

In short: replacing a1, a2 by their root mean square raises E[V] for every even V with V‴ ≥ 0 on the right, because such V is convex in x2 and the two densities differ in a +, −, + pattern with equal mass and second moment.

4 · FROM ROBIN HOOD TO ONE SIGN

How does one step become the whole theorem?

Lemma 2.1 compares two weights at a time. To reach the theorem the paper needs three more ingredients: a choice of V, a way to repeat the step until all weights are equal, and a way to turn expectations of V back into entropies. The choice is V = −log qn, the negative log-density of the equal-weight projection itself.

Fact · Proposition 2.2

Let n ≥ 150. If

Eq. 5

then the entropy inequality of Theorem 1.1 holds, with equality only when |ai| = 1/√n for all i.

In words: if the log-density of the balanced shadow has a negative third derivative on the right, the theorem follows. This criterion was observed by Bartczak, Nayar and Zwara; the paper supplies a complete proof of the reduction. With V = −log qn, Eq. 5 says V‴ ≥ 0, which is exactly the hypothesis of the Robin Hood lemma. The rest of the sum is Y = Σi≥3 aiUi, and the paper checks that adding uniforms one at a time keeps a density even and unimodal, so the lemma applies. (A technical detail: qn vanishes at ±√n, so the paper first works with V(ρx) for ρ < 1 and lets ρ increase to 1 at the end by monotone convergence.)

The repetition is a simple averaging scheme. At every step, take a largest and a smallest weight and replace both by their root mean square. In terms of the squared weights si = ai2, the largest x and the smallest y are both replaced by (x + y)/2, and the total stays 1. The paper measures progress by the sum of squared deviations from the target 1/n, which drops by exactly ½(x − y)2:

Proposition 2.2, averaging step

Every si lies between y and x, so the total deviation is at most n(x − y)2, and each step removes at least a fraction 1/(2n) of it:

Proposition 2.2

On the four-coin example the squared weights are (0.6, 0.2667, 0.0667, 0.0667), and the deviation from 1/4 is 0.1225 + 0.0003 + 0.0336 + 0.0336 = 0.19. The first step averages x = 0.6 and y = 0.0667 into 0.3333 each, removing ½(0.5333)2 = 0.1422 and leaving 0.0478, well under the guaranteed factor 1 − 1/8 = 0.875. The animation below runs the scheme to the end.

The last ingredient converts the inequality for E[V] into one for entropy. Iterating Lemma 2.1 and passing to the limit gives, for the starting weights a,

Eqs. 9 and 8

The right inequality is the averaging. The left one is the Gaussian-ceiling inequality from Section 2, h(f) ≤ Ef[−log g], used with g = qn instead of a Gaussian. The final equality holds because E[−log qn] under qn itself is its entropy. Equality in the first step forces f = qn, and the paper then uses the supports, [−Σai, Σai] against [−√n, √n], together with the equality case of Cauchy–Schwarz to conclude ai = 1/√n.

Animation · Robin Hood on four coins
current shadow densityequal-weight density q₄

The animation computes each density by repeated convolution on a grid, and the entropy h and the cross-entropy E[V] = E[−log q4(X)] by numerical integration. Two things are worth watching. The cross-entropy rises at every step and always sits above the entropy, as the chain of inequalities requires. And all of this is for n = 4, which the theorem does not cover; the run illustrates the mechanism but proves nothing about n = 4. These four-coin numbers are ours.

Fact · the reduction

After Section 2 of the paper, the entire theorem rests on one property of one function: the log-density of n−1/2(U1 + ⋯ + Un) has a nonpositive third derivative on (0, √n). The paper proves the strict inequality for every n ≥ 150.

This is a delicate property. For a Gaussian, log g(x) = −x2/2 + const, whose third derivative is identically zero. So Eq. 5 says that qn, which is very close to Gaussian for large n, deviates from it with a definite sign at third order, at every point of (0, √n) including the far tail. A Gaussian approximation alone cannot decide a sign whose Gaussian value is zero; the correction term has to be controlled.

In short: repeatedly averaging the largest and smallest squared weights converges to equal weights, the Robin Hood lemma makes E[−log qn] rise along the way, and Gibbs' inequality turns that into entropy, so everything reduces to (log qn)‴ ≤ 0.

5 · EXPONENTIAL TILTING

How can a sign at every point be checked at one point?

The condition must hold at every x in (0, √n), and near the edge of the support the density qn is tiny and far from Gaussian. The paper's way around this is exponential tilting, a tool from large deviations and saddlepoint approximation: reweight the uniform distribution so that the point of interest becomes the mean, where the central limit theorem works best. After rescaling (Eq. 10, (log qn)‴(x) = n3/2(log pn)‴(√n x)), it suffices to prove (log pn)‴(x) < 0 for 0 < x < n, where pn is the density of the unnormalized sum U1 + ⋯ + Un.

Definition · cumulant function and tilted uniform

Eq. 11

For t ∈ ℝ, the tilted uniform Ut has density ½ etu − K(t) on [−1, 1]. In words: multiply the flat density by etu, which favors the right end when t > 0, and divide by the constant that restores total mass 1. At t = 0 nothing changes.

The function K packages every moment of the tilted variable. Integrating against the tilted density gives E[esUt] = exp[K(t + s) − K(t)] (Eq. 12), and differentiating at s = 0 gives E[Ut] = K′(t) and Var(Ut) = K″(t) > 0. Explicitly,

Eq. 17

Since the mean increases strictly from 0 to 1, every target x ∈ (0, n) equals nE[Ut] for exactly one t > 0. At t = 1, for example, E[U1] = coth 1 − 1 ≈ 0.3130 and Var(U1) = 1 − 1/sinh21 ≈ 0.2759, so t = 1 handles the point x ≈ 0.3130n (our arithmetic).

derivationWhy is E[esUt] = exp[K(t + s) − K(t)]?

Integrate esu against the tilted density: ½e−K(t)∫−11e(t+s)u du. The integral is 2E[e(t+s)U] = 2eK(t+s), so the result is eK(t+s) − K(t). Expanding in s, the coefficient of s is K′(t), which is the mean, and log E[es(Ut − K′(t))] = K″(t)s2/2 + K‴(t)s3/6 + ⋯, so K″ is the variance and K‴ the third central moment.

∎

Now standardize: Y = (Ut − E[Ut])/√Var(Ut), so E[Y] = 0, E[Y2] = 1 and E[Y3] = K‴(t)/K″(t)3/2. Take n independent copies and let w be the density of W = n−1/2(Y1 + ⋯ + Yn). The tilt of a sum is the sum of the tilts, which the paper proves by induction on the number of summands: the sum of n independent copies of Ut has density etx − nK(t)pn(x). Comparing with the density of nE[Ut] + √(nVar(Ut)) W gives, for −n < x < n,

Eq. 15

Take logarithms. The factor enK(t) − tx contributes nK(t) − tx, which is linear in x, so it disappears after two derivatives. Differentiating three times and evaluating at the mean x = nE[Ut] leaves

Eq. 16

This is the point of tilting. The sign of (log pn)‴ at any x ∈ (0, n) equals the sign of (log w)‴ at 0, for the standardized sum built from the matching t. The condition at every point has become a condition at the center, for a one-parameter family of distributions.

proofWhy is the tilted sum's density etx − nK(t)pn(x)?

For one summand this is the definition, since p1 = ½ on [−1, 1]. Suppose the sum of j − 1 tilted copies has density etu − (j−1)K(t)pj−1(u). Given that this sum equals u, adding one more copy gives density ½et(x−u) − K(t) at x for |x − u| ≤ 1. Averaging over u, the exponentials combine to etx − jK(t), which does not depend on u, and what remains is ½∫x−1x+1pj−1(u) du = pj(x) by Eq. 13.

∎

Animation · tilting the four-coin sum
p₄, the untilted sumtilted sum etx−4K(t)p₄(x)one tilted summand

The animation uses n = 4 so that p4 can be drawn exactly (it is a piecewise cubic, the Irwin–Hall density rescaled to [−4, 4]). For each t it multiplies p4 by etx − 4K(t), checks that the result still has total mass 1, and marks its mean 4E[Ut]. The small inset shows one tilted summand on [−1, 1]. As t grows, the tilted sum slides toward the right edge and narrows, and its skewness E[Y3] grows more negative.

To decide the sign of (log w)‴(0), the paper separates the third derivative from the lower ones:

Eq. 18

For a standard Gaussian the bracket equals 3, since w′(0) = 0 and w″(0)/w(0) = −1. The paper also explains the right comparison constant with a formal Edgeworth argument: the first correction to the Gaussian is proportional to (x3 − 3x)e−x2/2, whose first and third derivatives at 0 are −3 and 15, suggesting w‴(0) ≈ −5w′(0). Any constant strictly between 3 and 5 can then separate the terms, and the paper chooses 7/2. It remains to prove, for every t > 0,

Section 3

Substituting into Eq. 18 then gives (log w)‴(0) < [w‴(0) + (7/2)w′(0)]/w(0) < 0.

derivationWhy do −3 and 15 appear?

The check is ours. Expand (x3 − 3x)e−x2/2 = (x3 − 3x)(1 − x2/2 + ⋯) = −3x + (5/2)x3 + ⋯. The first derivative at 0 is the coefficient of x, −3, and the third derivative is 3! times the coefficient of x3, which is 15. The ratio is −5, and the Gaussian part contributes 0 to both odd derivatives, so to leading order w‴(0)/w′(0) ≈ −5.

∎

In short: tilting by etu moves any point x ∈ (0, n) to the mean of a reweighted sum, so (log pn)‴(x) has the sign of (log w)‴(0); Eq. 18 and the constant 7/2 split that sign into three estimates on w(0), w′(0), w″(0) and w‴(0).

6 · DENSITY DERIVATIVES FROM SINES AND COSINES

How do we get our hands on w and its derivatives?

The density w has no simple formula, but its characteristic function does, because W is a normalized sum of independent copies of Y. Fourier inversion turns the four numbers w(0), w′(0), w″(0), w‴(0) into integrals of E[cos(uW)] and E[sin(uW)].

Definition · characteristic function

The characteristic function of W is E[eiuW] = E[cos(uW)] + iE[sin(uW)], and its modulus is ρ(u) = √(E[cos(uW)]2 + E[sin(uW)]2) (Eq. 25). In words: the average of a point spinning around the unit circle at speed u. If W were symmetric, the sine part would vanish; the sine part measures asymmetry.

For sums the characteristic function multiplies. The paper writes this out with trigonometric identities (Eq. 26) so that everything stays real. Inverting and differentiating under the integral, which the paper justifies with an explicit integrable bound, gives

Eq. 28

The two odd derivatives, which decide the sign, both come from the sine expectation. That is the quantity the rest of the paper estimates.

derivationWhere do these four formulas come from?

Fourier inversion gives w(x) = (1/2π)∫ e−iuxE[eiuW] du = (1/2π)∫ E[cos(u(W − x))] du, after taking real parts. Expanding cos(u(W − x)) = cos(ux)cos(uW) + sin(ux)sin(uW) and folding the even integrand onto u ≥ 0,

Each x-derivative brings down a factor u and swaps cos and sin with signs; at x = 0, sin(0) = 0 and cos(0) = 1 leave only the terms shown. The paper bounds each differentiated integrand by ujρ(u), which is integrable for j ≤ 3, so dominated convergence allows the differentiation.

∎

Decay. For a single tilted summand the paper computes E[cos(sUt)] and E[sin(sUt)] in closed form (Eqs. 22 and 23) and proves

Eq. 20 · Lemma 4.2

for every t and v, using a scalar inequality sin2s ≤ s2/(1 + s2/3) from Abi-Khuzam and the variance bound Var(Ut) ≤ 1/3. Multiplying n factors at v = u/√n gives ρ(u) ≤ (1 + u2/n)−n/2 ≤ rn(u) = (1 + u2/n)−(n−1)/2 (Eq. 27). For large n, rn(u) behaves like e−u2/2 near the origin but decays only like a power for large u, which is enough to make every integral in Eq. 28 finite once n is large. At t = 0 the summand is Y = √3U, its characteristic function is sin s/s with s = √3v, and Eq. 20 reduces to the scalar inequality (sin s/s)2 ≤ 1/(1 + s2/3) itself; this remark is ours.

Keeping the skewness. As t → 0 the tilted variable becomes symmetric, so E[Y3], w′(0) and w‴(0) all tend to 0. A bound on E[sin(uW)] that does not carry a factor E[Y3] would swamp the quantity being measured. The paper's key device is a one-sign-change lemma.

Fact · Lemma 4.3

Let ξ have density f, mean 0 and E|ξ|3 < ∞, and suppose that for some b ≥ 0, f(y) − f(−y) is nonnegative for 0 < y < b and nonpositive for y > b. Then E[ξ3] ≤ 0 and

Eq. 29

strictly when f is not even and v ≠ 0.

In words: if the density leans right near the center and left in the tail, then the sine expectation is controlled by the third moment alone. The tilted Y satisfies the hypothesis. Its density is increasing on its support, which runs from −(1 + E[Ut])/√Var to (1 − E[Ut])/√Var, so f(y) > f(−y) up to the right endpoint and f(y) = 0 beyond it (Eq. 32).

proofWhy does one sign change control every odd convex function?

Let h be odd and convex on [0, ∞). Since E[ξ] = 0, subtracting any multiple of y from h does not change E[h(ξ)]. Subtract the line through (0, 0) and (b, h(b)). Convexity with h(0) = 0 makes h(y)/y nondecreasing, so h(y) − yh(b)/b is ≤ 0 on (0, b) and ≥ 0 beyond b, the opposite signs to f(y) − f(−y). By oddness,

Eq. 30

Apply it to h±(y) = v3y3/6 ± sin(vy), which are strictly convex on y > 0 because h±″(y) = v2[vy ∓ sin(vy)] > 0. The two results combine into (v3/6)E[ξ3] + |E[sin(vξ)]| < 0, which gives both claims.

∎

The same comparison with φ(x) = x5/120 − x3/6 − sin x gives a lower bound (Lemma 4.5): E[sin(vY)] ≥ (1/6)|E[Y3]|v3(1 − 11v2/10). Here 11/10 comes from the moment bounds collected in Lemma 4.1,

Eq. 19 · Lemma 4.1

since 22/120 = 11/60 = (1/6)(11/10). The bound −2 ≤ E[Y3] comes from a result of Bubeck and Eldan on log-concave densities, and the ratio bound 22 from an explicit power series in Appendix A whose coefficients are all positive (Eq. 54). In our numerical check, E[Y3] is about −0.34, −0.68, −1.27, −1.89 and −2.00 at t = 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8, approaching −2, the skewness of a reflected exponential variable, as the tilt piles the mass against the right end.

The Gaussian prediction. The paper rescales the sine expectation by its natural size, Sn(u) = √n E[sin(uW)]/|E[Y3]| (Eq. 33). The central limit heuristic predicts Sn(u) ≈ (u3/6)e−u2/2, and Lemma 4.6 turns that into rigorous bounds valid for |u| ≤ √n/2:

Eq. 34

Eq. 35

The proof writes E[cos(uY/√n)] + iE[sin(uY/√n)] in polar form, so that the n-fold product has modulus ρ(u) and angle θ(u), bounds ρ from below by exp(−u2/2 − u4/(7n)) and from above by rn (Eq. 38), and bounds the angle by 4|E[Y3]|u3/(21√n) (Eq. 39) using Lemma 4.3. Every error term carries a factor 1/n.

The animation evaluates the exact characteristic function of W from Eqs. 11 and 12, φUt(s) = (t/sinh t)·sinh(t + is)/(t + is), raised to the n-th power after centering and scaling, and plots Sn against the Gaussian prediction. It then integrates Eq. 28 numerically to obtain w(0), w′(0), w″(0) and w‴(0) and reports (log w)‴(0). These computations are ours, and they were cross-checked against the exact Irwin–Hall density at n = 10 through Eq. 15. The paper proves bounds; the animation shows the actual values the bounds are protecting.

In short: Fourier inversion makes w′(0) and w‴(0) integrals of E[sin(uW)]; the one-sign-change lemma bounds that by the skewness, and Lemma 4.6 pins it near (|E[Y3]|/√n)(u3/6)e−u2/2 with errors of order 1/n.

7 · CLOSING THE ESTIMATES

Where does the number 150 come from?

With the bounds of Lemma 4.6 in hand, the three estimates of Section 3 become integrals that can be computed or bounded explicitly. The integrals split at u = √n/2: inside, the Gaussian-plus-error bounds apply; outside, everything is bounded crudely by rn. The tail pieces are controlled by the moment integrals

Eqs. 42 and 57

The recursion comes from one integration by parts, and M0(n) ≤ (2n − 3)/(2(n − 3)) from a polar-coordinates trick (Eq. 56). For a Gaussian the same integrals would be 1, 1, 3, 15, …; for n ≥ 150 Lemma B.1 gives M2 < 21/20, M4 < 5, M6 < 24, M10 < 1500 and M12 < 16000 (Eq. 55).

Fact · Proposition 4.7

For every n ≥ 150 and t > 0,

Eq. 43

and −3w″(0)/w(0) + 2w′(0)2/w(0)2 < 7/2 (Eq. 44).

The numbers are Gaussian values with room to spare: for the standard normal, w(0) = −w″(0) = 1/√(2π). The bracket bound follows by arithmetic: −w″/w < 21/19 and w′/w < 20|E[Y3]|/(19√n), with |E[Y3]| ≤ 2, give 63/19 + (8/n)(20/19)2, which is about 3.375 at n = 150 (our arithmetic), below 3.5. The positivity of w′(0) comes from the lower bound √(2πn)w′(0)/|E[Y3]| > 1/2 − 21/(4n) − 1500/(216n) − 1/(2n), about 0.415 at n = 150 against the paper's stated 2/5.

Fact · Proposition 4.8

For every n ≥ 150 and t > 0, w‴(0) + (7/2)w′(0) < 0 (Eq. 47).

The proof rewrites the combination with Eq. 28 as one weighted integral of Sn,

Eq. 48

and replaces Sn by its Gaussian prediction plus an error. The Gaussian part is exact: (1/6)·15 − (7/12)·3 = 3/4, from the Gaussian moments ∫u6e−u2/2/√(2π) = 15 and ∫u4e−u2/2/√(2π) = 3 (Eq. 49). The error is split at u = √14/2, where the weight changes sign, and at u = √n/2. The three pieces are bounded below by −1/20, −80/n (Eq. 50) and −1/10, so

Eq. 51

Here is where the dimension enters most visibly. The right side is 0.6 − 80/n, positive only when n > 133.3. At n = 150 it is about 0.067. Several other steps (the moment bounds, the tail estimates, the 2/5 and 19/20 bounds) also use n ≥ 150, so 150 is the threshold at which every explicit constant in the chain closes at once. The observation that Eq. 51 alone would allow n ≥ 134 is our arithmetic and does not by itself extend the theorem, because the other estimates were only checked for n ≥ 150.

Assembling: by Eq. 43, w(0) > 0 and w′(0) > 0; by Eq. 44 and Proposition 4.8, Eq. 18 gives (log w)‴(0) < 0 for every t > 0; by Eq. 16 this is (log pn)‴ < 0 at every point of (0, n); by Eq. 10, (log qn)‴ < 0 on (0, √n); and Proposition 2.2 delivers the entropy inequality and its equality case.

In short: the Gaussian contributes exactly 3/4 to the decisive integral, the errors cost at most 1/20 + 80/n + 1/10, and making every such constant close simultaneously is what requires n ≥ 150.

9 · ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what isn't

What is shown is a complete, self-contained proof of the Eskenazis–Nayar–Tkocz conjecture for cube projections in every dimension n ≥ 150, including the equality case. All constants are explicit and every inequality in the chain is proved in the text or its appendices. The reduction in Section 2 makes the Bartczak–Nayar–Zwara criterion rigorous, including the boundary issues at ±√n. The analytic core is a careful, quantitative central limit argument that keeps the skewness as a factor, which is necessary because the quantity being signed tends to zero as the tilt vanishes. Our independent checks agree with the paper where we tested them: the trapezoid sign pattern and second moments at (0.8, 0.6), the values of E[Ut] and Var(Ut), the arithmetic of Eqs. 43, 44 and 51 at n = 150, and the heuristic ratio w‴(0)/w′(0) ≈ −5, which our n = 150 computation puts at about −4.96.

What is not shown is the conjecture for 3 ≤ n ≤ 149. The paper states its result only for n ≥ 150 and does not discuss small dimensions or say whether the derivative condition (5) holds there. For n = 2 the conjecture follows from our closed form in Section 2, but that is not in the paper. Whether the method can be pushed lower is a question of sharpening constants: Eq. 51 alone would close at n = 134, but the other estimates were stated only for n ≥ 150, and by the paper's count of continuous derivatives (pn has n − 2 of them) the condition only makes sense for n ≥ 5. The result is also specific to uniform summands: the tilting computations use the explicit form of K(t) = log(sinh t/t) and the one-sign-change structure of the tilted uniform.

The paper is a single-author preprint posted on November 10, 2026, and has not yet been refereed.

A connection, oursExponential tilting is the same reweighting that underlies the Esscher transform in actuarial science and the change of measure used to price options or to simulate rare events by importance sampling: multiply a density by etx, renormalize with the cumulant function, and a rare region becomes typical. Here it is used not to compute a probability but to transfer a sign from the edge of the support to its center.

In short: a complete and fully explicit proof for n ≥ 150; dimensions 3 to 149 remain open in the paper, and the method is tailored to uniform summands.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.13533v1. Equation, lemma and proposition numbers match the paper. All three animations run real computations: the averaging scheme on four coins with densities by numerical convolution and entropies by numerical integration, the exact tilted Irwin–Hall density for n = 4, and the exact characteristic function of the standardized tilted sum with numerical Fourier integrals. The two-coin entropy formula and its monotonicity proof, the four-coin numbers, the derivation of the −3 and 15, the n = 134 remark, all numerical values of E[Y3] and of w and its derivatives, and the Esscher connection are ours.

Loss of the Quadratic Speedup in Grover Search under Local and Coherent Noise

Imama Tul Birrah Khan, Muhammad Faryad · posted Nov 12, 2026 · quant-ph · arXiv 2611.16398

Overview

Grover's algorithm finds one marked item among N in about √N steps by turning a state vector through a small angle again and again, and this paper works out, in closed form, exactly how noise takes that rotation apart. The answer comes in three shapes. Noise that scrambles the whole register leaves the rotation untouched but shrinks the part of the state that is rotating, by a fixed factor per gate layer. Noise on individual qubits knocks amplitude out of the two-dimensional plane where the search happens, and a short geometric fact says that whatever leaves the plane is frozen there for good. Coherent errors in the rotation angle keep the state pure but blur where it points, by an amount that grows linearly with depth. All three lead to the same rule of thumb: the total error accumulated over the √N-deep circuit must stay of order one, which for errors on single qubits means a per-qubit error rate below about 1/(n√N), where n is the number of qubits.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • why Grover's oracle and diffusion step are two reflections, why two reflections make a rotation by 2α with sin α = 1/√N, and where the π√N/4 iteration count comes from;
  • what a density matrix is, how a noise channel acts on one, and how bit flips, phase flips and depolarizing noise differ;
  • why a depolarizing channel on the whole register commutes with every gate, and how that gives the exact success probability Pr(pg) of Eq. 30;
  • why the best stopping point moves earlier under noise, and how the expected query cost goes from √N to about 2pgN;
  • why the Grover operator is just −1 off the search plane, and why that makes a phase flip most harmful early and a bit flip most harmful late;
  • how the in-plane part of the state obeys Bloch-type equations with leakage and dephasing rates, and where the noise budget p ≲ 1/(c n√N) comes from;
  • how bounded angle errors widen into a band of possible success probabilities that grows linearly with depth.
