Running examples
  • The ordinary cube Q3. Eight vertices, twelve edges, six square faces. It is small enough to check every claim by hand, and the first animation searches all 256 of its switchings. Its answer is F3 = 3.
  • The 4-cube Q4 and its special switching u. Sixteen vertices drawn as two copies of Q3. A single explicit ±1 labeling u of these vertices makes every vertex meet exactly one red edge, which gives F4 = 8. The same u is the building block of the whole paper.
  • The weighted square (r, 1). A single square with two edges of weight r and two of weight 1. For r = 2 it unfolds into Q5 and gives F5 = 24; for r = 3 it unfolds into Q10 and gives F10 = 1792. The third animation carries out both unfoldings vertex by vertex.
1 · RED AND BLUE SQUARES

What exactly is being minimized, and where does the question come from?

The n-cube Qn has the 2n bit strings of length n as vertices, with an edge between two strings when they differ in exactly one position. Each vertex has n neighbors, so there are n2n−1 edges. A square, or 4-cycle, is what you get by fixing all but two coordinates and letting those two vary over 00, 10, 11, 01. Every square uses edges in exactly two directions.

Erdős asked whether every subgraph of Qn with no square has at most (1/2 + o(1))n2n−1 edges, about half of all edges. The paper's starting point is a simple way to build large square-free subgraphs: color every edge red or blue so that each square has one or three red edges. Then neither color class contains a whole square, since a square entirely in blue would have zero red edges and one entirely in red would have four. If k edges are red, the blue edges form a square-free subgraph with n2n−1 − k edges, and the goal becomes making k as small as possible.

Definition · fully frustrated signing

A signing of a graph assigns each edge a sign, +1 or −1. The sign of a cycle is the product of the signs of its edges. A signing of Qn is fully frustrated when every square has sign −1.

In words: call the −1 edges red. A signing is fully frustrated exactly when every square face has an odd number of red edges.

The smallest case is a single square, Q2. It needs an odd number of red edges, and one is enough, so the minimum is 1. Already on Q3 the six faces interact, since each edge lies on two of them. A red edge can serve two faces at once, so one might hope that three red edges suffice for six faces, and on Q3 they do. Section 4 shows why fewer is impossible.

In short: color the n-cube's edges so every square has an odd number of red edges; the fewest red edges possible is the number Fn this paper studies, and the blue edges then form a large square-free subgraph.

2 · SWITCHING AND THE FRUSTRATION INDEX

Why is there one number Fn, rather than one per coloring?

There are many fully frustrated signings, and it is not obvious that they all have the same minimum. The tool that ties them together is switching. Switching at a vertex reverses the sign of every edge at that vertex. A cycle through the vertex uses exactly two of those edges, so its sign is multiplied by (−1)2 = 1. Switching therefore never changes the sign of any cycle, and in particular it keeps a fully frustrated signing fully frustrated.

Switching at a set of vertices is conveniently described by a Boolean function f: vertices → {−1, 1}, switching at the vertices where f(x) = −1. An edge xy then has its sign multiplied by f(x)f(y), because it is reversed once for each endpoint that is switched.

Definition · frustration index

The frustration index of a signed graph is the minimum number of edges meeting every negative cycle, or equivalently the minimum number of negative edges over all switchings of the signing.

In words: how few red edges you can reach by repeatedly flipping all the edges at chosen vertices.

Fact · all fully frustrated signings are equivalent

Because the squares generate the cycle space of Qn, any two fully frustrated signings of Qn differ only by switching. Their common frustration index is Fn, the minimum possible number of red edges, and a fully frustrated signing with exactly Fn red edges is called optimal.

our sketchWhy does "the squares generate the cycle space" imply that two such signings differ by switching?

The paper states this in one sentence; the argument below is ours, written out for completeness. Take two fully frustrated signings σ and σ′ and multiply them edge by edge, τ = σσ′. Every square has sign (−1)(−1) = +1 under τ. Saying that the squares generate the cycle space means that every cycle can be built from squares by repeatedly taking symmetric differences of edge sets, and a sign that is +1 on each building block is +1 on the result, because edges used twice contribute a square factor. So τ is +1 on every cycle.

Now fix the vertex 0 and define f(x) as the product of τ along any path from 0 to x. Two paths to x form a closed walk, whose τ-sign is +1, so f is well defined. For an edge xy, the path to y can go through x, so f(y) = f(x)τ(xy), which says τ(xy) = f(x)f(y). Hence σ′ = στ is σ switched by f.

∎

To compute anything we need one concrete fully frustrated signing. The paper uses the canonical signing, in which the edge from x to x ⊕ ei has sign (−1) raised to x0 + ⋯ + xi−1, the number of ones strictly before position i. Edges in direction 0 are always blue. On a square in directions i < j, flipping bit i changes the sign of the direction-j edges, while flipping bit j leaves the sign of the direction-i edges alone. The two direction-j edges of the square therefore have opposite signs and the two direction-i edges have equal signs, so the square has sign −1. The canonical signing has (n − 1)2n−2 red edges, since each direction other than 0 has half its 2n−1 edges red.

On Q3, writing vertices as x0x1x2, the canonical signing has four red edges: 100–110 and 101–111 in direction 1, and 100–101 and 010–011 in direction 2. That matches (3 − 1)21 = 4. Switching at the vertex 100 reverses its three edges. Two of them were red and become blue, and the blue edge 000–100 becomes red, leaving three red edges. The animation below checks these counts and then tries all 28 = 256 switchings to confirm that three is the minimum.

Animation · switching the 3-cube
red edge, sign −1blue edge, sign +1switched vertex

The number inside each vertex is its signed degree, the number of blue edges at that vertex minus the number of red ones. That number will turn out to be the right way to think about the whole problem.

The physics reading

Put a spin sx = ±1 on every vertex and give each edge a coupling Jxy = σxy/√n, where σ is the fully frustrated signing. The Ising energy H(s) = −Σedges Jxysxsy rewards a blue edge whose spins agree and a red edge whose spins disagree. A spin configuration is the same thing as a switching f = s, and an edge is "unsatisfied" exactly when it is red after switching. No configuration satisfies every edge, because every square is negative, which is why physicists call the model fully frustrated. The paper records that the ground-state energy per vertex is −μn/(2√n), with μn defined in Section 3. This model was studied by Derrida, Pomeau, Toulouse and Vannimenus in 1979 and later by Marinari, Parisi and Ritort.

The following link is ours, not the paper's. Minimizing an Ising energy over ±1 spins is the problem quantum annealers and QUBO solvers are built for; the substitution sx = 1 − 2bx turns it into a quadratic function of 0/1 variables. The fully frustrated hypercube is therefore a natural hard benchmark whose exact optimum is now known in many dimensions.

our derivationWhere does −μn/(2√n) come from?

The sum Σedges σxysxsy counts each edge once, while sTAns counts each edge twice, once from each end. So H(s) = −sTAns/(2√n). Dividing by the 2n vertices gives −⟨An⟩s/(2√n), whose minimum over s is −μn/(2√n).

∎

In short: switching flips all edges at a vertex and never changes a cycle's sign; every fully frustrated signing of Qn is a switching of the canonical one, so Fn is the fewest red edges reachable by switching, and it is also a ground-state energy.

3 · THE SIGNED ADJACENCY MATRIX

How does linear algebra turn red-edge counting into an eigenvalue problem?

Counting red edges after a switching is a quadratic expression in the switching function f, and quadratic expressions are what matrices are for. The paper introduces one operator per direction.

Definition · signed adjacency operators

In words: the operator Γi fetches the value of f at the neighbor across the direction-i edge and multiplies it by that edge's canonical sign. The parity operator Pd negates f on odd-weight vertices. The signed adjacency matrix An is the ordinary adjacency matrix of the cube with each entry multiplied by the sign of its edge.

Four algebraic facts carry the paper. Each Γi is symmetric, and Γi2 = I, because crossing the same edge twice multiplies by its sign twice. For i ≠ j, the operators anticommute, ΓiΓj = −ΓjΓi, because the two routes around an (i, j)-square have opposite sign products; this is full frustration written as algebra. Finally each Γi anticommutes with the parity operator, since crossing any edge changes parity. Squaring the sum, the cross terms cancel in pairs and only the squares survive.

Eq. 2.1

Eq. 2.1 is stated for weighted sums Γw = ΣwiΓi, which Section 5 will need; with all weights equal to one it says An2 = nI. A symmetric matrix whose square is nI has only the eigenvalues √n and −√n.

On the single square Q2, order the vertices as 00, 10, 01, 11 (writing x0x1). The only red canonical edge is 10–11, so

The off-diagonal entries of A22 count the two length-2 walks between opposite corners, and they cancel precisely because one of the two walks crosses the red edge. Without the red edge they would add to 2, and the square of the ordinary adjacency matrix is not a multiple of the identity.

A connection worth knowing

Ordering vertices by their first coordinate, the paper writes An in block form as An−1 on the diagonal, −An−1 in the other diagonal block, and identity matrices off the diagonal (Section 5 and Lemma 2.1). This is exactly the recursively defined matrix in Hao Huang's 2019 proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture, which used An2 = nI and Cauchy interlacing to show that any 2n−1 + 1 vertices of Qn induce a subgraph with a vertex of degree at least √n. The paper cites the related work of Mathews and of Laplante, Naserasr, Sunny and Wang; the identification with Huang's matrix is ours.

Now count red edges. After switching by f, the edge xy has sign f(x)σxyf(y). The quadratic form fTAnf adds up these switched signs, counting each edge twice. If k edges are red, this sum is 2(n2n−1 − 2k). The local field h(x) = f(x)(Anf)(x) is the signed degree of x after switching, and its average over the 2n vertices is ⟨An⟩f = n − 4k/2n. Solving for k and maximizing over f gives the paper's dictionary.

Eq. 1.4

In words: the frustration index Fn is determined by the largest possible average signed degree μn, and fewer red edges means a larger average. The last inequality is the Rayleigh bound, fTAnf ≤ √n · ‖f‖2 = √n · 2n, since √n is the largest eigenvalue.

derivationWhy does the Rayleigh bound hold for a symmetric matrix?

This is a standard linear algebra fact, included as background. A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors v1, …, vm with eigenvalues λ1, …, λm. Writing f = Σcjvj, we get fTAf = Σλjcj2 ≤ λmaxΣcj2 = λmax‖f‖2. Equality needs f to lie entirely in the top eigenspace. A Boolean f has ‖f‖2 = 2n, and λmax = √n here.

∎

Combining the two halves of Eq. 1.4 gives Fn ≥ (n − √n)2n−2, the spectral lower bound. It is the same bound Bialostocki proved in 1983 by other means. On the running examples: the cube Q3 has F3 = 3, so μ3 = 3 − 3 · 4/8 = 1.5, below √3 ≈ 1.732. On Q4, Section 6 exhibits an f with every signed degree equal to 2, so μ4 = 2 = √4 and F4 = (4 − 2) · 4 = 8: the spectral bound is met exactly.

In short: the signed adjacency matrix satisfies An2 = nI, the number of red edges after switching by f is (n − mean signed degree)2n−2, and therefore Fn = (n − μn)2n−2 with μn ≤ √n.

4 · A PARITY BOUND

Can the spectral bound be improved using the fact that degrees are integers?

The spectral bound would be met only if every signed degree equaled √n exactly. When √n is not an integer that is impossible, and the paper squeezes extra information out of this. Three facts about the local field h of any switching hold simultaneously.

Fact · Lemma 3.1, integer local-field bound

For every Boolean f on Qn, with h(x) = f(x)(Anf)(x),

Consequently, if r is a positive integer of parity opposite to n, then μn ≤ (n + r2 − 1)/(2r), which by Eq. 1.4 is

Eq. 1.1

Equality holds exactly when every local field is r − 1 or r + 1, and then the fraction of vertices with field r + 1 is [n − (r − 1)2]/(4r) in each parity class.

In words: a signed degree is a sum of n signs, so it has the parity of n. Its mean is the quantity we want to make large, and its mean square is pinned at n by Eq. 2.1. A distribution of integers with fixed mean square and a forbidden value r has its mean pushed down, and the best case is when every value sits right next to r.

proofHow do the parity and the second moment combine into Eq. 1.1?

Since h(x) and r have opposite parity, h(x) − r is odd, so (h(x) − r)2 ≥ 1 at every vertex. Average over vertices and expand: 1 ≤ ⟨h, h⟩ − 2r⟨h, 1⟩ + r2 = n − 2r⟨An⟩f + r2. Rearranging gives ⟨An⟩f ≤ (n + r2 − 1)/(2r) for every f, hence for the maximum μn.

Equality forces (h(x) − r)2 = 1 everywhere. If a fraction α of vertices has field r + 1, the second moment gives n = (1 − α)(r − 1)2 + α(r + 1)2 = (r − 1)2 + 4rα, which solves to the stated fraction. The two parity classes have the same size and the same total signed degree, because every edge contributes its sign once to each class; with only two possible values, the proportions must agree in both.

∎

The best r is the integer of the right parity that minimizes (n + r2 − 1)/(2r), which is near √(n − 1). The interesting case is n = r2 + 1, where the bound on μn becomes 2r2/(2r) = r, strictly below the spectral value √(r2 + 1), and Eq. 1.1 reads Fn ≥ (n − r)2n−2 = (r2 − r + 1)2r²−1. In this case the fraction of field r + 1 is exactly one half.

Check it on Q3. Here n = 3 is odd, so take r = 2: the bound gives μ3 ≤ 6/4 = 1.5 and F3 ≥ (3 − 1.5) · 2 = 3. The switching at 100 found in the animation reaches 3, so F3 = 3, and the equality condition predicts what the animation shows: every signed degree is 1 or 3, and the fraction with degree 3 is (3 − 1)/8 = 1/4 in each parity class, one vertex out of four. The mean square is (2 · 9 + 6 · 1)/8 = 3 = n, as Lemma 3.1 requires. For Q5 = Q2²+1, the bound is F5 ≥ (5 − 2) · 8 = 24, and equality would need half the vertices at signed degree 3 and half at 1.

The bound has a long history. The paper attributes the averaging argument to Derrida et al., and notes that the earlier construction of Brass, Harborth and Nienborg, shown by Laplante et al. to give a fully frustrated signing in every dimension, attains it in dimension r2 + 1 when r is a power of two or r = 3. The new theorem is that it is attained for every r.

In short: signed degrees have the parity of n and mean square n, so they cannot all equal a value r of the other parity; this gives Eq. 1.1, which in dimension r2 + 1 says F ≥ (r2 − r + 1)2r²−1, with equality exactly when every signed degree is r ± 1.

5 · WEIGHTED CUBES

Where would a switching with every signed degree equal to r ± 1 come from?

Proving the lower bound is tight means building, in every dimension r2 + 1, a switching whose signed degrees are all r − 1 or r + 1. The paper's idea is to find this pattern first on a tiny graph where it is obvious, and then transport it.

Consider one square. Give its two horizontal edges sign + and weight r, and its two vertical edges opposite signs and weight 1. The weighted signed degree, the sum of incident signs counted with their weights, is r + 1 at the two vertices on the positive vertical edge and r − 1 at the two on the negative one. Those are exactly the two values Eq. 1.1 asks for on Qr²+1, and they occur half the time each. The question the paper asks is how to realize this on a cube where every edge has weight one.

Definition · weighted cube and local field

For a weight vector w = (w0, …, wd−1), the weighted adjacency operator on Qd is Γw = Σi wiΓi, so Γ(1,…,1) = Ad. After switching by f, the local field and its mean are

In words: the local field is the weighted signed degree after switching, each direction-i edge counting wi instead of 1.

Eq. 2.1 still holds, so the mean square of the local field is ‖w‖22. For the square with weights (r, 1) and f the constant function 1, the canonical signing gives h(x) = r + (−1)x0: direction 0 is always positive and contributes r, and direction 1 has sign (−1)x0. For r = 2 the fields are 3, 3, 1, 1, with mean 2 and mean square (9 + 9 + 1 + 1)/4 = 5 = 22 + 12.

This suggests the strategy. The mean square of the local field on a weighted cube is ‖w‖22, and on an ordinary cube it is the dimension n. So a weighted cube with ‖w‖22 = n is a compressed picture of Qn, and the paper's lifting turns this picture into an actual switching of Qn with the same distribution of local fields. The weights (r, 1) have r2 + 1 as their squared norm, which is how that dimension enters.

In short: on a square with weights (r, 1), the all-ones switching already has local fields r ± 1 in equal numbers; the rest of the paper is about unfolding a weighted cube with ‖w‖22 = n into Qn without changing its local fields.

6 · ONE PERFECT SWITCHING OF Q4

How can a weight 2 be split into four weights 1?

The simplest unfolding replaces one coordinate of weight 2b by four coordinates of weight b, so the squared norm is unchanged, (2b)2 = 4b2. To make it work we need, on Q4, a switching that behaves like "weight 2 in a single direction": every vertex should have signed degree exactly 2. That is a Boolean eigenfunction of A4 with eigenvalue 2, and the paper builds one from the 3-cube.

Let η be the indicator of the two vertices 000 and 111 of Q3, and put g = A3η. The vertices 000 and 111 are not adjacent, and every other vertex of Q3 has exactly one neighbor among them. So g vanishes on {000, 111} and equals ±1 everywhere else, the sign of the unique edge leading into the set. It follows that both g + η and g − η are Boolean. Since A3g = A32η = 3η, direct multiplication gives

When the first bit of Q4 indexes the two blocks, the displayed matrix is A4: direction 0 contributes the identity blocks, and the other three directions have their canonical signs reversed in the block where x0 = 1. So u = (g + η, g − η) is a Boolean function on Q4 with A4u = 2u.

checkWhere exactly does the first block row give 2(g + η)?

The first block row computes A3(g + η) + (g − η) = A3g + A3η + g − η = 3η + g + g − η = 2g + 2η. The second computes (g + η) − A3(g − η) = g + η − A3g + A3η = g + η − 3η + g = 2g − 2η. Both rows agree with 2u.

∎

Concretely, writing Q3 vertices as x1x2x3, the values of g are 0 at 000 and 111, −1 at 101, and +1 at the other five vertices. So u equals −1 at exactly four vertices of Q4, namely x0x1x2x3 = 1000, 0101, 1101 and 1111, and +1 elsewhere. Switching the canonical signing at those four vertices takes the red-edge count from 12 to 8, and every vertex ends up with exactly one red edge, so the red edges form a perfect matching. The animation builds u in these steps and verifies every signed degree.

Animation · building u on Q4
red edgeblue edgeη = 1, or u = −1

With u in hand, the first refinement is a short formula. Let π(x) be the parity of |x| for x in Q4. For a function f of one bit, define (Tf)(x) = u(x)f(π(x)). On the one-bit cube with weight 2b, the constant function 1 and the function s ↦ (−1)s are eigenfunctions of Γ(2b) with eigenvalues 2b and −2b. Their images under T are u and P4u, and these are eigenfunctions of bA4 with the same eigenvalues, because A4u = 2u and A4P4 = −P4A4. So bA4T = TΓ(2b): applying the weighted operator and then unfolding is the same as unfolding and then applying the ordinary one.

For the running example, take the square with weights (2, 1) and f = 1, whose fields are 3 at the two vertices with x0 = 0 and 1 at the two with x0 = 1. Unfolding the weight-2 coordinate into four bits gives a function on Q5, namely u applied to the first four bits. Every source field is copied to 25−2 = 8 vertices, so Q5 gets 16 vertices of signed degree 3 and 16 of signed degree 1. The mean is 2, and Eq. 1.4 gives (5 − 2)23 = 24 red edges, meeting the bound of Section 4. Hence F5 = 24.

In short: from the two antipodal corners of Q3 the paper builds a ±1 function u on Q4 with A4u = 2u; it gives F4 = 8 directly, and the map Tf = u · f(parity) unfolds a weight 2b into four weights b while copying every local field.

7 · THE LIFTING THEOREM

Which weighted cubes can be unfolded into ordinary cubes?

The four-way refinement only handles even weights. For the weights (3, 1) needed in dimension 10, the paper uses a second replacement, and then shows that the two together unfold exactly the weight vectors one could hope for.

Definition · the two refinements, Lemma 2.1

with b > 0 in the first case and a > b > 0 in the second. Both preserve the squared norm. For each there is a linear isometry T from functions on the old cube to functions on the new one that sends Boolean functions to Boolean functions and satisfies Γw′T = TΓw and Pd′T = TPd. In particular ⟨Γw′⟩Tf = ⟨Γw⟩f.

In words: either replacement can be carried out on any switching, giving a switching of a bigger cube with the same mean local field, and the parity condition makes it safe to do this to one block of coordinates inside a larger cube.

The squared norms match because 2((a + b)/2)2 + 2((a − b)/2)2 = a2 + b2. For the pair refinement the paper reuses u. Split the four directions of Q4 into two pairs, L = Γ0 + Γ1 and R = Γ2 + Γ3, and set v = (L − I)u. Then L2 = R2 = 2I and RL = −LR, and together with (L + R)u = 2u these give

so the refined operator Γw′ = ((a + b)/2)L + ((a − b)/2)R acts by Γw′u = au + bv and Γw′v = bu − av. Those are the same formulas by which Γ(a,b) acts on the two-bit functions 1 and χ(s, t) = (−1)s. The map T then sends 1 to u and χ to v: at each vertex x of Q4 it reads off a source vertex (s(x), t(x)) of the square, with (−1)s(x) = u(x)v(x) and t(x) = s(x) ⊕ π(x), and sets (Tf)(x) = u(x)f(s(x), t(x)).

proofWhy is v Boolean, so that T sends ±1 functions to ±1 functions?

At each vertex x the four numbers u(x)(Γiu)(x) are signs whose sum is u(x)(A4u)(x) = 2. So exactly one of them is negative. The sum of the first two is therefore 0 or 2, and u(x)v(x) = u(x)(Lu)(x) − 1 is −1 or 1. Since u is Boolean, so is v.

To check one of the four relations: Lv = L(L − I)u = 2u − Lu = u − v. And Rv = R(L − I)u = −LRu − Ru = −L(u − v) − (u − v) = −u − v, using Ru = (L + R)u − Lu = 2u − (u + v) = u − v.

∎

proofWhy is every such map automatically an isometry that copies each vertex the same number of times?

Both maps have the form (Tf)(x) = ε(x)f(φ(x)) with ε(x) = ±1. Grouping target vertices by their source φ(x) shows that T*T is diagonal, with entry ρ(y) = 2d−d′|φ−1(y)| at the source vertex y. The symmetry of both weighted operators and the intertwining identity give ΓwT*T = T*Γw′T = T*TΓw. Reading off the entry at an edge yz gives Γw(y, z)ρ(z) = ρ(y)Γw(y, z), and since the weights are positive, ρ(y) = ρ(z). The cube is connected, so ρ is constant; it averages to one because the preimages partition the target cube. So T*T = I and every source vertex has exactly 2d′−d preimages.

To refine coordinates in the middle of a longer weight vector, the paper first moves them to the front with signed swaps (Sf)(x) = (−1)xixi+1f(τx), which exchange two adjacent weights, and then uses Γw = Γα ⊗ I + Pk ⊗ Γβ for a block α of length k followed by the rest β. The parity identity Pk′T = TPk is what lets T ⊗ I intertwine the second term.

∎

Repeating the refinements gives the central result. Call a linear map T from functions on Qd to functions on Qn a lifting of w if it preserves Boolean functions and AnT = TΓw.

Fact · Theorem 2.2, Boolean lifting

A weight vector w with positive real entries admits a lifting to Qn if and only if its entries are integers and

Every lifting is an isometry. If the local field of a Boolean f takes a given value at m vertices of Qd, the local field of Tf takes that value at 2n−dm vertices of Qn. In particular ⟨An⟩Tf = ⟨Γw⟩f.

proofWhy do the refinements always reach all-ones weights when the conditions hold?

Whenever a weight is even, say 2b, replace it by four copies of b. If all weights are odd and two differ, a > b, apply the pair refinement; the half-sum and half-difference of two odd numbers are integers. The weights stay positive integers with squared norm n.

Both refinements preserve the common odd divisors. An odd number divides 2b exactly when it divides b. If it divides a and b it divides (a ± b)/2, since 2 is invertible modulo an odd number, and conversely a and b are the sum and difference of the new weights. So the greatest common odd divisor stays 1.

Each step increases the number of weights, which can never exceed n because the weights are positive integers whose squares sum to n. So the process stops, and it can only stop when all weights equal the same odd value. That value has no odd divisor larger than 1, so it is 1, and there are exactly n of them.

∎

proofWhy are the integer and gcd conditions necessary?

Take any lifting T. In one row of its matrix, flipping the sign of one input changes the output by twice the corresponding entry; both outputs are ±1, so each entry is 0 or ±1. Choosing the input signs to match the nonzero entries shows their absolute values sum to 1. So each row has a single nonzero entry, and (Tf)(x) = ε(x)f(φ(x)). The entries of AnT are integers, while row x of TΓw contains the weights w0, …, wd−1 at the neighbors of φ(x); hence the weights are integers. Squaring the intertwining identity and using Eq. 2.1 gives nT = ‖w‖22T, so n = ‖w‖22.

For the gcd, the paper proves that every Boolean s on Qn and every coordinate j satisfy

Eq. 2.2

The reason is that ΓjAn = I + Σi≠jΓjΓi, and each ΓjΓi with i ≠ j is skew-symmetric, so its quadratic form vanishes; what remains is sTs = 2n. If an odd prime p divided every weight, then s = T1 would satisfy Ans = TΓw1 ≡ 0 modulo p at every vertex, making the left side of Eq. 2.2 divisible by p. But 2n is not.

∎

The gcd condition has teeth. The single weight w = (3) has squared norm 9, and the constant function on its one edge has local field 3 at both ends. If it could be lifted, Q9 would have a switching with every signed degree 3 and F9 = (9 − 3)27 = 768. The odd common divisor 3 forbids it, and Section 10 shows that F9 is in fact 772. This reading of w = (3) as the obstruction is ours; the paper makes the corresponding argument directly in Proposition 5.4.

The animation runs the refinement procedure from the proof on the weighted square (r, 1). At every step it rebuilds the switching on the new, larger cube, recomputes every local field from scratch with the canonical signs, and counts how often each value occurs. At the end it counts red edges one by one.

Animation · unfolding the weighted square
weightsfield r + 1field r − 1

For r = 3 the procedure first applies the pair refinement to (3, 1), giving (2, 2, 1, 1), and then splits each 2 into four 1s, ending with ten coordinates of weight 1. The two field values 4 and 2 each occupy exactly 512 of the 1024 vertices, as Theorem 2.2 promises.

In short: two refinements, 2b → (b, b, b, b) and (a, b) → ((a+b)/2, (a+b)/2, (a−b)/2, (a−b)/2), each carry switchings along with their local fields; together they unfold a weight vector into Qn exactly when its entries are integers with squared norm n and power-of-two gcd.

8 · EXACT VALUES

What does the lifting theorem give in dimension r2 + 1 and nearby?

All the work has been done, and the main theorem now takes a few lines.

Fact · Theorem 1.1

For every positive integer r,

Eq. 1.2

If 4 divides r and p ∈ {±1, ±2, ±3}, then

Eq. 1.3

In both cases equality holds in Eq. 1.1.

proofHow do Sections 4 to 7 combine to prove Eq. 1.2?

Put n = r2 + 1. On the square with weights (r, 1), the constant function has local field r + (−1)x0. The weights are coprime and their squares sum to n, so Theorem 2.2 lifts this function to Qn with the same two field values r ± 1. Since n and r have opposite parity, Lemma 3.1 says this is optimal, and Fn = (n − r)2n−2.

∎

For the six neighboring dimensions the paper starts instead from a weighted cube whose local field is constant. Lemma 3.2 supplies two of them: the weight vectors (2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1) and (3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1), whose squares both sum to 16 and which both carry a Boolean eigenfunction with eigenvalue 4. The first comes from u by doubling all four weights and splitting one of the 2s. The second repeats the construction of u with the length-seven Hamming code in place of {000, 111}: the code is a set C of vertices of Q7 such that no two are adjacent and every vertex outside C has exactly one neighbor in C, so g = A7η is again 0 on C and ±1 off it, and the block matrix with A7, 3I, 3I, −A7 sends (g + η, g − η) to four times itself.

proofHow does changing one weight by 1 reach the dimensions r2 + 1 + pr/2?

Let 4 | r, put k = r/4 and n = r2 + rp/2 + 1, which is odd, so Lemma 3.1 bounds μn ≤ (n + r2 − 1)/(2r) = r + p/4. Choose a vector w from Lemma 3.2 with an entry wj = |p| and its eigenfunction f with eigenvalue 4. Scaling the weights by k makes the local field 4k = r and the squared norm 16k2 = r2. Now change kwj to kwj + ε with ε the sign of p. Its square changes by 2kp + 1, so the new squared norm is r2 + 2kp + 1 = n, and the new local field is r + εf(x)(Γjf)(x), which is r ± 1 at every vertex.

An unchanged weight k survives, and k is coprime to kwj + ε, so the gcd is 1. The only zero weight arises for r = 4 and p = −1, that is n = 15, where the paper restricts f to the face xj = 0 and drops that direction. Theorem 2.2 lifts the function to Qn with local fields in {r − 1, r + 1}, and Lemma 3.1 gives μn = r + p/4.

∎

With r = 4 these give Fn in every odd dimension from 11 to 23, as the paper notes. Evaluating Eqs. 1.2 and 1.3 ourselves: F11 = 3968, F13 = 19456, F15 = 92160, F17 = 425984, F19 = 1933312, F21 = 8650752 and F23 = 38273024. The animation's r = 4 run reproduces F17 = 425984 by counting red edges on all 131072 vertices of Q17. In the dimensions of Eq. 1.3 the proportions of the two signed degrees are 1/2 + p/8 and 1/2 − p/8.

The construction also has freedom, which the paper uses to answer a question of Reza Naserasr about which Boolean functions arise from optimal signings. In an optimal signing of Qr²+1, g = h − r is a balanced ±1 function. Proposition 3.3 shows that for odd r ≥ 3 the lift can be chosen so that every coordinate has influence 1/2 on g, meaning half the edges in each direction join vertices of different signed degree, and g has sensitivity n/2 at every odd-weight vertex. The proof identifies g with Ambainis's four-bit function, which is −1 exactly when its four input bits are in nondecreasing or nonincreasing order. Corollary 3.4 strengthens this for r = 2k ± 1 ≥ 3: every vertex then has n/2 neighbors of each signed degree.

In short: lifting the square (r, 1) gives a switching of Qr²+1 with all signed degrees r ± 1, so the parity bound is tight and Fr²+1 = (r2 − r + 1)2r²−1; nudging one weight of two 16-norm cubes covers six more dimensions around each r2 + 1 with 4 | r.

9 · EVERY DIMENSION

How close to the spectral bound can one get when n is not of the special form?

Between consecutive values r2 + 1 there are about 2r dimensions not covered by Theorem 1.1. The paper first shows that μn can only grow with n.

Eq. 4.1

Take two copies of an optimal fully frustrated signing of Qd, and join each vertex x to its copy by an edge of sign (−1)|x|. A new square uses two joining edges at adjacent vertices, which have opposite signs, and two copies of one old edge, which have equal signs, so it is negative. Half the joining edges are positive, so they add nothing to the mean local field, which stays μd. Theorem 1.1 gives μr²+1 = r, and monotonicity then gives μn ≥ ⌊√(n − 1)⌋, so √n − μn is bounded. The paper sharpens this.

Fact · Theorem 1.2

There is an absolute constant C such that for every n ≥ 1,

The order of the error is best possible: Theorem 1.1 gives √(r2 + 1) − μr²+1 = 1/(√(r2 + 1) + r), which is of order 1/√n.

In words: the spectral lower bound is off by at most C/√n in the coefficient of 2n−2, and nothing better than order 1/√n is possible in general. The uniform upper bound of Laplante et al. had coefficient n − (2√2/3)√n + O(n−1/2), so the paper improves the constant in front of √n from 2√2/3 ≈ 0.943 to 1.

proof ideaHow does varying one weight close the gap between r2 + 1 and n?

Let r = 2q be the largest even integer with r2 + 1 ≤ n and Δ = n − r2 − 1 ≤ 8q + 3. If Δ < 80, monotonicity and Eq. 1.2 already give √n − μn ≤ √n − r ≤ 40/r. Otherwise, the paper lifts the square (r, 1) only partway, splitting r into four copies of q and using the refinements (Lemma 4.1) to manufacture a coordinate j of a chosen weight a = ⌊(Δ − 64)/16⌋. Increasing that weight by 8 adds 16a + 64 to the squared norm, which lands within 15 of n, and adds 8⟨Γj⟩f to the mean local field.

The estimate of that increase uses Eq. 2.1 twice. First, ‖(Γw − rI)f‖2 = (r2 + 1) − 2r2 + r2 = 1. Second, since ΓjΓi is skew-symmetric for i ≠ j, ⟨Γjf, Γwf⟩ = wj = a. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives |a − r⟨Γj⟩f| ≤ 1, so the mean rises by at least 8(a − 1)/r. Combining with √n − r ≤ (8a + 40)/r gives √n − μn ≤ 48/r, and r ≥ √n − 2 finishes the proof after enlarging C for small n.

∎

Taking the positive edges of an optimal signing gives a subgraph whose complement, the red edges, is also square-free, since every square has edges of both signs. This returns to Erdős's question.

Fact · Corollary 1.3

For every n ≥ 1 there is a subgraph G of Qn such that both G and its edge complement are C4-free and |E(G)| ≥ (n + √n − C/√n)2n−2. In the dimensions of Eqs. 1.2 and 1.3 the construction gives ex(Qr²+1, C4) ≥ (r2 + r + 1)2r²−1 and ex(Qn, C4) ≥ (n + r + p/4)2n−2.

Bialostocki proved that in any red-blue coloring of Qn with no monochromatic square, each color class has at most (n + √n)2n−2 edges, so Corollary 1.3 determines the largest such color class Bn up to O(n−1/2) in the coefficient. In the concluding remarks the paper also proves (Proposition 6.1) that in the dimensions of Theorem 1.1, Bn = n2n−1 − Fn exactly, and every maximizing coloring has no square with two opposite edges of each color.

For physics, the ground-state energy per vertex −μn/(2√n) of Section 2 tends to −1/2, as Parisi and Potters conjectured, and Theorem 1.2 gives the rate: the error is O(1/n).

In short: μn never decreases in n, and by fine-tuning one weight in a partial lift of (r, 1) the paper shows Fn = (n − √n + O(n−1/2))2n−2 in every dimension, which also gives square-free subgraphs whose complements are square-free with about (n + √n)2n−2 edges.

10 · DIMENSION NINE

When n is a perfect square, why does the spectral bound sometimes fail, and by how much?

When n = r2, a constant signed degree r passes both tests of Lemma 3.1: it has the parity of n and mean square n. So the parity bound gives nothing beyond the spectral bound (n − r)2n−2, and the question is whether that bound is attained. For Q4 it is, by the switching u. For Q9 the spectral bound is 6 · 27 = 768. Marinari, Parisi and Ritort reported an energy corresponding to 772 red edges, an explicit switching with 772 is available, and the paper proves nothing smaller exists.

The tool is the residual of a switching, which measures its distance from the ideal. Suppose s gives (n − r)2n−2 + δ red edges and set q = (Ans − rs)/2. At a vertex with local field h(x), qx = s(x)(h(x) − r)/2. Since h(x) ≡ r modulo 2, q has integer entries, and An2 = r2I gives Anq = −rq. So q is an integer vector in the −r eigenspace. Its length records the excess δ.

Eq. 5.1

The middle step uses Σh(x)2 = 2nr2 from Lemma 3.1 and Σh(x) = r2n − 4δ from counting edges. For Q9, with r = 3, ruling out 768, 769, 770 and 771 red edges means ruling out residuals of squared length 0, 6, 12 and 18. A zero residual would mean A9s = 3s, which Eq. 2.2 forbids because 3 does not divide 29.

Fact · Lemma 5.3

Let n = r2 with r ≥ 3. Every nonzero integral vector q with Anq = −rq satisfies ‖q‖22 ≥ 2r2, with equality precisely when q = ±(An − rI)ez for some vertex z.

In words: the shortest integer vectors in the bottom eigenspace are the "stars", with −r at one vertex and ±1 at its n neighbors, of squared length r2 + n = 2r2. For Q9 that length is 18, so 769 and 770 are excluded at once, and 771 requires the residual to be a star.

proof outlineWhy can't a shorter integer eigenvector exist?

Split q = (u, v) by the first coordinate, putting the half of smaller squared length k first; the block form of An gives v = −ru − Cu with C = ±An−1, and expanding yields ‖q‖2 = 2r(rk + uTCu) = 2ra with a a positive integer and k ≤ ra (Eq. 5.2). Lemma 5.1 bounds the restriction of Ad to any t vertices: its operator norm is at most √(t − 1), because in its square the length-2 walks between distinct vertices cancel in pairs when both middle vertices are present. That gives a ≥ k(r − √(k − 1)) (Eq. 5.3), which exceeds r for 2 ≤ k ≤ n − 2.

If ‖q‖2 ≤ 2r2, then a ≤ r, so k is 1, n − 1 or n. The case k = 1 gives exactly a star. In the other two cases Eq. 5.4 forces at least r(k − 1)/2 negative edges inside the support of u after switching, but negative edges there form a bipartite graph with no 4-cycle, and Lemma 5.2 caps such a graph on t vertices at t(1 + √(2t − 3))/4 edges. The two requirements contradict each other for r ≥ 3.

∎

Fact · Proposition 5.4 and Theorem 1.4

Equality in the spectral bound Fn ≥ (n − √n)2n−2 holds if and only if n is a power of four. If r ≥ 3 is not a power of two,

Eq. 5.5

With r = 3 this gives F9 ≥ 6 · 27 + 4 = 772, and the explicit switching gives equality: F9 = 772.

proofWhy can't the residual be a star?

For the first claim: equality forces a Boolean s with Ans = √n s, so √n = r is an integer; then Eq. 2.2 gives 2n = r(Γis)Ts, so r divides 2n and is a power of two. Conversely, for r a power of two, Theorem 2.2 lifts the constant function on the one-edge cube of weight r.

For Eq. 5.5, Eq. 5.1 and Lemma 5.3 give 2rδ ≥ 2r2, so δ ≥ r. If δ = r, the residual is a star, (An − rI)s = 2ε(An − rI)ez, so s′ = s − 2εez satisfies Ans′ = rs′ and differs from a ±1 vector only at z. Because AnPn = −PnAn, the vector Pns′ lies in the −r eigenspace and is orthogonal to s′, which says the squared entries of s′ sum to the same value on the two parity classes. Both classes have 2n−1 vertices, so the entry at z must also have square 1, and s′ is a Boolean eigenvector with eigenvalue r. That contradicts the first claim. So δ ≥ r + 1. For even r, every switching of Qr² has an even number of red edges, which pushes δ to r + 2.

∎

Two consequences are worth stating. The largest edge set of Q9 meeting every square in an odd number of edges has 9 · 28 − 772 = 1532 edges, which answers a question of Minamoto, who asked whether 1536 were possible. And Parisi and Potters' conjecture that the ground-state energy equals −1/2 whenever n is a square holds only for powers of four, since the energy is −1/2 exactly when the spectral bound is attained. The next open square dimension is 25, for which the paper records, without proof, 167 772 180 ≤ F25 ≤ 168 230 912.

In short: in square dimensions the excess over the spectral bound is the squared length of an integer eigenvector divided by 2r; the shortest ones are stars, a star cannot come from a switching unless r is a power of two, and so F9 = 768 + 4 = 772.

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved in the paper. Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, Corollary 1.3, Proposition 5.4 and the lower bound F9 ≥ 772 come with complete proofs, and the proofs are short and checkable. The lifting theorem is an if-and-only-if, so it also explains why the method cannot directly reach some dimensions. The constructions are explicit: every optimal signing in Theorem 1.1 is given by a sequence of refinements, which the animation above carries out for r = 2, 3 and 4 and which match Eq. 1.2 exactly.

Relied on from outside. The upper bound F9 ≤ 772 is not constructed in the paper. It rests on an explicit switching with 772 red edges posted as an edge list (reference [2], credited to "Bil812") and on the energy reported by Marinari, Parisi and Ritort. The matching lower bound is the paper's contribution. A reader who wants to verify the equality has to check that edge list.

Stated without proof. The bounds 167 772 180 ≤ F25 ≤ 168 230 912 are recorded without proof, with only a description of where they come from. The claim that some constant C < 1 is admissible in Theorem 1.2 is also asserted, with the remark that it follows from refining the estimates and checking small dimensions; the proof given yields an unspecified constant (48/r for large n before small cases are absorbed).

Open. The exact value of Fn outside the families of Theorem 1.1 and outside powers of four, starting with n = 25; whether C = 2 − √2, the value forced by μ2 = 1, suffices; and Erdős's original question, which is about all square-free subgraphs, not only those whose complement is also square-free. Corollary 1.3 gives a lower bound for it but does not resolve it.

Process. The author states that OpenAI Codex was used to explore proof strategies, check arguments, run computations, search the literature and help draft the manuscript, and that the author reviewed the material and takes responsibility for it. Every proof we followed for this chapter checked out, and our independent computations agree with every formula we could test.

Controlling Avalanche Sizes in the Abelian Sandpile Model

Maike C. de Jongh, Antal A. Járai, Richard J. Boucherie, M.N.M. van Lieshout · posted Nov 11, 2026 · math.OC · arXiv 2611.15549

Overview

If you may pay a fixed price β to pick one grain of sand off a pile before each new grain lands, the best long-run strategy on a line of sites is to sweep a central stretch clean and leave the rest alone, and that stretch grows by exactly one site on each side every time β drops below the next triangular number k(k + 1)/2. The pile is the Abelian sandpile, the standard toy model of systems that build up stress slowly and release it in sudden cascades, like earthquakes, forest fires or crashes. The paper turns "should I intervene?" into a Markov decision process, a probability model with a controller in it, and solves it with one idea used over and over: every grain carries a price, equal to the number of future topplings it will cause on average, and that price is an expected hitting time of a random walk. On the graphs the paper solves, once the prices are known, the optimal policy can be read off by comparing prices with β.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • how the sandpile works: grains land at random, a site with as many grains as neighbors topples, and an avalanche is the cascade that follows;
  • why the graph Laplacian Δ describes toppling, and why its inverse, the Green's function G, tells you how big avalanches are on average (Eqs. 9 to 11);
  • what a Markov decision process is, and what the gain and bias of a policy measure (Eqs. 4 to 8);
  • why never intervening is optimal exactly when β is at least the largest grain price φ(a) (Theorem 3.3, Eq. 13);
  • what a local intervention policy and a topple-free set are, and how the controlled pile reduces to an uncontrolled pile on a smaller, contracted graph (Theorems 3.4 to 3.8);
  • how grain conservation and random walks give the long-run cost of such a policy in closed form (Theorem 3.9, Eq. 20), and how a price function certifies optimality (Theorem 3.10);
  • the complete answer on a line, βk = k(k + 1)/2 (Theorem 4.5), and the answers for the complete graph and the star.
